title: Postoperative DWI morphology and neurological worsening after eloquent-area glioma surgery: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Purpose To assess whether the association between postoperative diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and neurological worsening after eloquent-area glioma surgery differs according to lesion morphology. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 139 consecutive patients undergoing resection of eloquent-area supratentorial gliomas (WHO 2-4). Postoperative MRI (< 48 h) classified lesions as sector- or rim-shaped. Neurological status was assessed at discharge and 4-6 months. Results DWI lesions occurred in 44/139 patients (31.7%; 31 sector-shaped, 13 rim-shaped); 59 (42.4%) worsened at discharge. Overall, DWI positivity alone was not associated with worsening. Sector-shaped DWI lesions were associated with neurological worsening (positive predictive value, PPV of 58.1%) and remained associated after multivariable adjustment (OR 3.83, 95% CI 1.30-11.29), although the confidence interval was wide and the unadjusted association was borderline. Rim-shaped lesions carried a PPV of 38.5%, comparable to the risk in DWI-negative patients (37.9%), and the two morphologies did not differ significantly in direct comparison. Awake craniotomy was also independently associated with worsening, and frontal site with a lower risk. 61% of worsening occurred with negative DWI. A deficit was present at the 4-6 month follow-up in 9 patients (6.5%), all with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and was associated with a ≥ 50% evoked-potential decrease. Conclusion In this cohort, postoperative DWI positivity was associated with neurological worsening mainly when the lesion was sector-shaped, a finding that requires confirmation in larger series. Rim-shaped lesions showed a risk of worsening similar to that of a negative scan. Most worsening occurs without DWI ischemia, suggesting non-ischemic mechanisms of function-guided surgery. A deficit at follow-up occurred only in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma and was associated with intraoperative neurophysiological changes.

title: Improving the fairness and robustness of deep learning classification models through bias mitigation and post hoc calibration.
abstract: Purpose The goal of this study was to enhance the fairness and clinical applicability of deep learning models for classifying Alzheimer's disease from structural MRI scans. To achieve this, we addressed two key challenges: age-related bias and unreliable probability estimates. Specifically, we investigated in-processing debiasing strategies to achieve age-invariant predictions while preserving diagnostic accuracy. We also systematically evaluated post hoc calibration methods to improve the reliability, interpretability, and clinical usefulness of predicted probabilities across diverse patient populations. Methods Structural MRI data from three independent cohorts (ADNI, AIBL, and DELCODE) were preprocessed using a standardized pipeline. Age-related bias was addressed using two in-processing strategies, adversarial training (CF-Net) and GLM-based feature residualization (PMDN), implemented in a shared 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) framework. Additionally, post hoc calibration was performed using four regression methods: logistic, probit, isotonic, and Bayesian binning. We evaluated model performance, fairness, and calibration using classification as well as calibration-specific metrics. Results PMDN achieved the best overall performance, with higher balanced accuracy (0.71) and improved calibration (Brier ≈ 0.22), showing substantially reduced variability compared to baseline and CF-Net. PMDN effectively removed age-related bias, achieving near-zero age prediction correlation; CF-Net, however, showed only partial and unstable debiasing. Post hoc calibration further improved probability reliability, with nonparametric methods (isotonic regression and Bayesian binning) yielding the lowest calibration errors (MCE ≈ 0.21-0.24). Conclusion This study shows that, although deep learning models achieve similar classification performance, they differ significantly in terms of calibration, stability, and fairness. PMDN provides more consistent and effective age bias mitigation than the CF-Net approach, particularly in clinically relevant subgroups. Post hoc calibration improves probability reliability further, with nonparametric methods achieving the best calibration.

title: MRI and proton MR spectroscopy in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: a comprehensive imaging review.
abstract: Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) remains a leading cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability. Although cranial ultrasound is widely used as a bedside screening tool, brain MRI has become central to diagnosis, injury pattern classification, timing estimation, and outcome prediction. Furthermore, proton MR spectroscopy ( 1 H-MRS) provides complementary metabolic biomarkers that enhance prognostication. This review focuses on MRI and 1 H-MRS in neonatal encephalopathy due to hypoxic-ischemic injury, addressing both term and preterm infants. The pathophysiologic determinants of injury distribution are summarized, the optimal timing of imaging and diffusion evolution is discussed, and practical acquisition protocols including recommended sequences and 1 H-MRS parameters are proposed. Key MRI phenotypes in term infants-basal ganglia-thalamus injury, watershed/parasagittal cortical-subcortical injury, and global or near-total injury patterns are reviewed with attention to common pitfalls such as diffusion pseudonormalization and evolving T1/T2 signal changes. For preterm infants, this review highlights distinctive vulnerabilities of the germinal matrix and periventricular white matter, emphasizing the spectrum from punctate white matter injury (WMI) to cystic periventricular leukomalacia (PVL). For 1 H-MRS, voxel selection, echo time considerations, and interpretation of lactate, N-acetylaspartate (NAA), choline, creatine, and myo-inositol are detailed. Evidence suggests that deep gray matter lactate/NAA or NAA-based metrics serve as reliable and robust outcome biomarkers. Emerging directions including arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion are also discussed.

title: Comparison of PMAneo and RAPID in acute ischemic stroke: agreement in CT perfusion analysis and DEFUSE 3 imaging eligibility.
abstract: Purpose Automated computed tomography perfusion (CTP) analysis plays a key role in triaging acute ischemic stroke (AIS). This study aimed to evaluate the agreement of PMAneo compared with RAPID in a multicenter setting. Materials and methods We retrospectively reviewed 99 patients with anterior circulation AIS from three stroke centers using four different CT scanners. CTP data were processed using both PMAneo and RAPID. Volumetric agreement for ischemic core volume and Tmax > 6 s volume was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analysis. Multivariable regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with volume discrepancies. EVT imaging eligibility was evaluated according to the DEFUSE 3 criteria (ischemic core volume < 70 mL, mismatch ratio ≥ 1.8, and absolute mismatch volume ≥ 15 mL), using RAPID as the comparator. Results Ischemic core volumes showed excellent agreement between the two platforms (ICC = 0.881, 95% CI 0.827-0.918), and Tmax > 6 s volumes showed good agreement (ICC = 0.761, 95% CI 0.283-0.896), whereas mismatch volumes showed moderate agreement (ICC = 0.661, 95% CI 0.146-0.844). For the ischemic core threshold (< 70 mL), PMAneo demonstrated 100% (95% CI 96-100%) relative sensitivity and 67% (95% CI 38-88%) relative specificity. For the full DEFUSE 3 criteria, the relative sensitivity and specificity were 81% (95% CI 70-89%) and 84% (95% CI 66-95%), respectively. Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated proportional bias, with PMAneo underestimating volumes relative to RAPID as lesion size increased. Basal ganglia involvement and imaging site were significantly associated with these volume differences (p < 0.05). Conclusion PMAneo showed high volumetric agreement and comparable DEFUSE 3 imaging eligibility to RAPID, suggesting it is a reliable alternative for automated CTP analysis. Although proportional bias and potential diagnostic discrepancies were observed in borderline cases near clinically relevant thresholds, PMAneo may facilitate broader access to automated CTP analysis.

title: MRI-defined parametrial venous invasion in locally advanced cervical cancer: association with pathological venous invasion, pretreatment lymph node metastasis, and survival outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate MRI-defined parametrial venous invasion (mrPMVI) for detecting pathological parametrial venous invasion (pPMVI) and its associations with pretreatment lymph node metastasis (LNM) and survival outcomes in locally advanced cervical cancer. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 42 patients with cervical cancer with parametrial invasion on MRI or histopathology, corresponding to International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics 2018 stage IIB or higher disease. Fifteen patients underwent surgery without preoperative therapy and were included in the pathological validation analysis. Image interpretation was primarily based on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging. Two radiologists independently assessed mrPMVI using a five-point scoring system. Scores ≥ 3 were predefined as mrPMVI-positive. Diagnostic performance for pPMVI and interobserver agreement were evaluated. Univariable logistic and Cox regression analyses were performed for pretreatment LNM and survival outcomes, respectively. Results pPMVI was present in 10 of 15 patients. The five-point mrPMVI score showed an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.87 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.60-0.98) for detecting pPMVI. The predefined threshold (≥ 3) yielded 30.0% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Interobserver agreement for the five-point mrPMVI score was substantial (linearly weighted κ = 0.75). mrPMVI positivity was associated with pretreatment LNM (odds ratio = 4.00, 95% CI: 1.05-15.26, p = 0.042). During a median follow-up of 24.0 months, 16 patients experienced disease progression and 10 died. mrPMVI positivity was associated with shorter progression-free survival (hazard ratio = 34.25, 95% CI: 4.35-269.91; p < 0.001) and overall survival (hazard ratio = 10.16; 95% CI: 1.28-80.61, p = 0.028). Conclusion The mrPMVI score showed potential for identifying pPMVI, although the predefined threshold was highly specific but insensitive. mrPMVI positivity was associated with pretreatment LNM and survival outcomes, suggesting potential complementary value for risk characterization in locally advanced cervical cancer.

title: A Hybrid Human-AI Workflow for Ultrasound Report Quality Control: A Multicenter Performance and Efficiency Evaluation.
abstract: Rationale and objectives This study evaluated a hybrid human-AI workflow for ultrasound report quality assurance using multicenter retrospective data. Materials and methods 786 anonymized ultrasound reports covering 22 examination categories were collected from four hospitals. Reports containing naturally occurring or implanted errors were matched across arms. GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 performed initial screening before review by six human reviewers (HRs). HR with blinded expert over-reading (HR-ex) served as control. Accuracy, false-positive (FP) and false-negative (FN) rates, and review time were compared. Supplementary validation compared HR and DeepSeek-assisted review using 1680 consecutive reports without implanted errors. Results Hybrid workflow (HYB) accuracy was comparable to HR (4o-HYB 80.2%, v3-HYB 82.5%, HR 82.3%) but lower than HR-ex (87.3%). Both HYBs showed higher FN rates than HR-ex (4o-HYB 34.2% and v3-HYB 27.3% vs HR-ex 16.9%, both p < 0.001). Severity assessment did not indicate preferential omission of clinically significant errors. Human verification reduced LLM-generated FNs and FPs. Median review time decreased substantially from 51.0 s (HR-ex) to 11.0 s (4o-HYB) and 12.0 s (v3-HYB). In supplementary validation (error prevalence, 9.6%), v3.2-HYB and HR showed FN rates of 22.6% and 24.3%, FP rates of 7.7% and 10.0%, and median review times of 15.4 and 24.3 s, respectively. Conclusion The LLM-assisted HYB achieved accuracy comparable to single-physician review while substantially reducing audit time. These findings require prospective real-world validation before routine clinical implementation.

title: A natural neuronal receptor-derived MRI probe targets β-amyloid oligomers for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Early-to-mid detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains challenging because clinically used amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) probes primarily visualize fibrillar β-amyloid (Aβ) deposits and require radioactive isotopes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers a radiation-free alternative, but its application in molecular AD diagnosis is limited by insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration and poor specificity toward early-to-mid Aβ species. Here, we developed a BBB-crossing liposomal MRI probe, Lipo@D1D2-Gd, by integrating a natural Aβ oligomer-binding receptor domain with a gadolinium chelator. The extracellular D1D2 domains of human leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor B2 (LilrB2), a neuronal receptor that recognizes neurotoxic Aβ oligomers, were recombinantly produced and bioorthogonally conjugated with a gadolinium chelator. The resulting D1D2-Gd retained its Aβ-binding capability and MRI contrast activity. To enable brain delivery, D1D2-Gd was encapsulated within maltose-functionalized PEGylated liposomes designed to facilitate BBB transport. After intravenous administration to 4-month-old 5xFAD mice, Lipo@D1D2-Gd crossed the BBB, accumulated in Aβ-rich brain regions, and generated MRI contrast enhancement that differentiated 5xFAD mice from wild-type controls. Systemic safety evaluation showed no obvious hematological, biochemical, or histological toxicity. This study establishes a receptor-derived, BBB-crossing biomaterial platform for radiation-free molecular imaging of early-to-mid AD-associated Aβ pathology. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: 1) Promising Targeting Strategy: We repurposed a human-derived natural receptor domain (LilrB2 D1D2) as a targeting module for β-amyloid (Aβ) oligomers, a key pathogenic species in Alzheimer's disease (AD). 2) Non-invasive MRI Approach: We constructed a liposomal probe designed to deliver the Gd-labeled targeting agent to the brain, enabling the detection of Aβ-associated pathology in 4-month-old 5xFAD mice via non-radioactive MRI, well before overt cognitive decline. 3) Experimental Validation: We demonstrate the probe's association with Aβ oligomers/plaques, effective BBB crossing, differences in MRI signals between AD model and wild-type mice, and an initially favorable biosafety profile, with no observed toxicity under the tested conditions. 4) Clinical Translation Potential: Our work presents a promising pathway toward a safe, accessible, and early-to-mid-stage AD screening tool, with the potential to facilitate population-wide screening and earlier therapeutic intervention.

title: Oral squamous cell carcinoma: A modern review of pathogenesis and treatment.
abstract: Oral cancer (OC), predominantly oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), is a serious global health burden with high mortality rates, especially in South and Southeast Asia. OC is a severe worldwide health issue that is mostly caused by a sedentary lifestyle, alcohol, tobacco, and areca nut intake. The highest prevalence of OSCC is in India and Southeast Asia. Complex genomic and epigenetic changes, such as TP53 dysfunction, enhanced EGFR alteration, and dysregulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways, in conjunction with tumor-promoting alterations in the tumor microenvironment, contribute to oral carcinogenesis ( Tan et al., 2023). Oral submucous fibrosis (a chronic condition that causes precancerous progression in mouth), and leukoplakia (white or gray patches to form on mucus membrane) are instances of oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs), which are key indicators of cancer conversion. Even with advances in histopathology and imaging, delayed diagnosis remains a major limitation. Salivary biomarkers, liquid biopsy devices, and artificial intelligence-based screening tools are examples of novel diagnostic methods with potential for early diagnosis. Therapeutically, novel approaches such as immunotherapy, targeted therapy, nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, electro spun nanofibers, and plant-derived phytoformulations offer innovative, multi-targeted strategies with enhanced efficacy and reduce toxicity. However, surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy continue to be the primary treatment approaches. Improving new interventions for OC treatment needs a multifaceted approach that integrates early detection strategies, advanced therapeutic strategies, the use of plant-derived therapeutics, nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and public health awareness to get better therapeutic outcomes.

title: Contralateral piriform cortex alterations after surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy: A pilot MRI volumetry study.
abstract: Purpose Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is increasingly conceptualized as a network disorder, with the piriform cortex as an implicated region. We characterized postoperative contralateral piriform cortex-cortical amygdala (PCA) structural and perfusion-related changes in a small seizure-free TLE cohort. Methods Nine patients with drug-resistant TLE who underwent epilepsy surgery and achieved postoperative seizure freedom were included in this single-center pre-post pilot study. Bilateral PCA was manually delineated on 3D T1-weighted MRI using ITK-SNAP, and volumes were normalized to total intracranial volume derived from CAT12 segmentation. Eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal lobe regions were examined as exploratory regional-specificity comparisons. In patients with available pulsed arterial spin labeling (PASL), piriform and putaminal signal intensities were measured by region-of-interest analysis. Non-parametric paired tests were used; secondary and exploratory analyses were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure. Results Normalized to total intracranial volume (TIV) contralateral PCA volume decreased postoperatively (Wilcoxon Z = -2.073, exact two-tailed p = 0.039; r = 0.69). None of the eight atlas-derived contralateral temporal regions showed a significant pre-post volume change. Contralateral putamen-normalized piriform signal intensity did not change significantly (Z = -0.105, p = 0.917), and no secondary or exploratory analysis remained significant after FDR correction. Conclusions In this hypothesis-generating pilot cohort, contralateral PCA volume decreased after epilepsy surgery, whereas the PASL-derived signal-intensity measure did not show a corresponding group-level change. These observations do not establish a surgery-induced network mechanism and require confirmation in larger controlled longitudinal cohorts.

title: Bicentric comparison of 3-year clinical outcomes between endoscopic ultrasound-guided embolization with coil and hemostatic adjunct versus balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration for treatment of bleeding gastric varices: A propensity-score matched study.
abstract: Background and aims Endoscopic ultrasound-guided coil injection (EUS-COIL) and balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) performed by interventional radiology (IR) are both effective obliterative procedures to treat gastric varices. Comparative studies are lacking. Our aim was to assess clinical outcomes for EUS-COIL versus BRTO for treatment of acute gastric variceal bleeding. Methods This retrospective cohort study included all patients admitted to two tertiary care centers between 2009-2024 who underwent either EUS-COIL or BRTO for bleeding gastric varices. The primary outcomes were technical/clinical success and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included transfusions, reintervention, length of hospital stay, further hepatic decompensation (esophageal variceal hemorrhage, new ascites, or new hepatic encephalopathy (HE)), and all-cause mortality. Subgroup analyses were performed in patients with cirrhosis, including with propensity score matching (PSM) which was conducted 1:1 for age, sex, Child-Pugh classification, MELD-Na score, and hemoglobin level on admission. Outcomes over the 36-months post-intervention were assessed using time-to-event analysis. Results A total of 94 patients were included (48 EUS-COIL, 46 BRTO), of whom 60 patients with cirrhosis (30 per group) were analyzed after propensity score matching. In the matched cohort, technical success was 100% in both groups and clinical success was 100% versus 93.3% (p=0.49). The EUS-COIL group experienced significantly fewer adverse events (3% vs 37%; p=0.003) and had a longer time-to-reintervention (65 ± 52 days vs 10 ± 9.6 days; p=0.022) over a median follow-up 900 ± 790 days. The incidence of further hepatic decompensation was lower in the EUS-COIL group (10% vs 40%; p=0.007), as was the likelihood of further hepatic decompensation (HR 0.28 (95%CI: 0.08-0.984), p = 0.047) compared to BRTO. No significant differences were observed with regard to post-procedural transfusion requirements, rates of reintervention, length of hospital stay, and mortality in cirrhosis patients. In the unmatched cohort, technical (100% vs 80%; p=0.001) and clinical (100% vs 89%; p=0.03) success were higher with EUS-COIL than BRTO. Conclusions In patients with gastric variceal hemorrhage, EUS-COIL demonstrated higher rates of technical/clinical success and lower rates of adverse events (both peri-procedural and on long-term follow-up) compared to BRTO. EUS-COIL had significantly lower rates of further hepatic decompensation. While larger prospective studies are required, these data suggest that EUS-COIL, when available, may be the preferred initial therapy for bleeding gastric varices as part of a step-up strategy.

title: Pediatric Laryngeal Tumors: A Systematic Review of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms.
abstract: Background Pediatric laryngeal tumors are exceptionally rare and encompass a heterogeneous spectrum of benign and malignant neoplasms. Evidence remains largely limited to case reports and small case series. Objective To systematically characterize the histopathology, clinical presentation, treatment, recurrence, and outcomes of benign and malignant laryngeal tumors in children. Methods A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from January 2000 to July 2026 involving patients aged ≤18 years with histologically confirmed primary laryngeal tumors. Results Eighty-six studies were included. Among 52 patients with benign tumors, granular cell tumor was the most frequent diagnosis, followed by neurofibroma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. Hoarseness was the predominant symptom, and surgery, particularly endoscopic resection, was the principal treatment. Recurrence occurred in 7/44 patients (15.9%) with available outcome data. Among 69 patients with malignant or intermediate tumors, squamous cell carcinoma predominated, followed by sarcomas and lymphomas. Treatment included surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy according to histology and disease extent. Total laryngectomy was performed in nine patients, and 12 deaths were reported. Conclusions Pediatric laryngeal tumors are rare, but should be considered in children with persistent or progressive hoarseness, dyspnea, dysphagia, or other unexplained upper airway symptoms. Granular cell tumor and neurofibroma were the predominant benign lesions, whereas squamous cell carcinoma was the most frequently reported malignant neoplasm. Given the rarity of these tumors and the current reliance on case-based evidence, the establishment of international multicenter registries is warranted to generate higher-quality data and inform standardized diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms for pediatric laryngeal neoplasms.

title: Multi-omics liquid biopsy for leptomeningeal metastases in lung cancer: from molecular mechanisms to precision diagnosis and treatment.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM), a serious complication of advanced lung cancer, poses significant challenges in both clinical diagnosis and treatment monitoring, and is associated with a poor prognosis. Conventional diagnostic methods include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology; however, their sensitivity is limited, particularly in the early stages of the disease. Against this backdrop, liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive and practical approach for molecular assessment and longitudinal monitoring of LM. Recent studies have reported that, in selected cohorts of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and LM, CSF-derived circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) detects driver and resistance-associated alterations more frequently than paired plasma, while epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM)-based CSF circulating tumor cell (CTC) assays have reported sensitivities of 76%-100% and specificities of 84%-100%, compared with a first-lumbar-puncture sensitivity of 44%-67% for conventional CSF cytology. These performance estimates should be interpreted in the context of selected cohorts and heterogeneous reference frameworks. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid circulating tumor cell (CSF-CTC) burden holds prognostic value, with higher CTC levels associated with poorer survival outcomes. This review summarizes recent advances in liquid biopsy biomarkers including ctDNA, DNA methylation, microRNA (miRNA), proteins, and circulating tumor cells (CTCs), focusing on their applications in the diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and prognostic assessment of lung cancer-associated LM, and provides a comparative discussion of liquid biopsy based on plasma and cerebrospinal fluid specimens. It further explores the potential, current challenges, and directions for clinical translation of multi-omics integration in the personalized management of LM.

title: Multicenter external validation of a multimodal MRI deep-learning model to predict meningioma bone invasion.
abstract: Background Preoperative detection of meningioma bone invasion lacks objective biomarkers and relies on subjective radiological assessment, posing a risk of excessive bone resection or residual tumor. We therefore developed and externally validated a parsimonious six-feature DenseNet121 signature derived from multiparametric MRI across two independent institutions. Methods In this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 438 consecutive patients (mean age, 53 ± 11 years; 77% women) with histologically confirmed meningioma were allocated to training (n = 182), internal validation (n = 77), and external test (n = 179) sets. Following N4 bias-field correction and isotropic resampling, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted volumes were fed into a DenseNet121 architecture to extract a six-feature signature via nested cross-validation. Discrimination (area under the ROC curve, AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision-curve analysis) were evaluated. Results In the external cohort (prevalence 11%), the signature achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73-0.91), sensitivity 75%, specificity 77% and negative predictive value 96%, with an AUC improvement of 0.155 over conventional radiomics (95% CI, 0.01-0.30; p = 0.035). At a 20% risk threshold, decision-curve analysis confirmed a positive net clinical benefit, primarily driven by the high negative predictive value. SHAP analysis demonstrated the dominant and consistent contribution of low-ADC features. Conclusion The DenseNet121-derived six-feature signature serves as a reliable rule-out aid for preoperative meningioma bone invasion, with a high negative predictive value that may safely support decisions to avoid extensive bone resection in predicted-negative cases. Positive predictions require confirmatory CT or intraoperative biopsy to mitigate false positives. This tool could assist nurses and surgeons in preoperative planning, facilitating personalized patient care and potentially reducing operative time and complications.

title: A hierarchical residual Swin transformer with dual-level locality compensation for accelerated MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides high spatial resolution, excellent soft-tissue contrast, and reliable anatomical discrimination, and is therefore widely used in clinical diagnosis. However, long acquisition time still limits imaging efficiency and clinical throughput. Although convolutional neural network (CNN)-based deep learning approaches have shown considerable promise for reconstructing images from undersampled k-space data, existing methods frequently fail to preserve fine structural details and texture continuity under aggressive undersampling conditions. In this study, we propose a novel reconstruction network based on the Swin Transformer, which integrates three key components: (i) long residual connections to facilitate the recovery of high-frequency details; (ii) a dual-level locality compensation mechanism to restore local spatial information; and (iii) a channel recalibration module to explicitly capture global dependencies among channels, thereby enhancing global feature extraction. Extensive experiments conducted on the IXI and MICCAI 2013 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms several compared generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches for MRI reconstruction across all undersampling mask types, achieving a PSNR improvement of approximately 0.6-1 dB over the best competing method under various settings. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/cvgjhuor/HR-SwinGAN.

title: Therapeutic potential and toxicological trade-offs of nanoparticle-enhanced valproic acid in glioblastoma: Behavioral and oxidative insights.
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with a poor prognosis. In the current research, the therapeutic and behavioral efficacy of valproic acid (VPA) and its nanoparticles (Nano VPA) with or without temozolomide (TMZ) was investigated in the C6 glioblastoma rat model. Methods We divided eighty-four adult male Wistar rats into seven groups (n = 12/group): sham, tumor, TMZ, VPA, nano VPA, VPA + TMZ, and nano VPA + TMZ. To induce tumors, C6 cells were injected into the brains of the rats. On days 12 to 15, behavioral performance was assessed using the social interaction test, elevated plus maze, open field, rotarod, and passive avoidance. On day 18, tumor size, edema, and histopathology were examined. Oxidative stress parameters in brain tissue and serum were measured by ELISA. Results VPA and Nano VPA significantly inhibited tumor growth, either alone or with TMZ. All treatments except Nano VPA + TMZ improved survival compared with tumor controls. Treated groups showed enhanced anxiety regulation, sociability, learning, and memory. Motor coordination improved following VPA or Nano VPA therapy. Tumor induction reduced serum SOD, CAT, and TAC levels; treatments raised serum TAC and lowered brain MDA, but further reduced serum SOD. Conclusion Our results suggest that oxidative stress modulation may contribute to the neurobehavioral and antitumor effects of both VPA and nano-VPA. While nano-VPA showed greater tumor reduction, conventional VPA was more effective in improving survival. Combining VPA with TMZ may enhance outcomes, and support further study of Nano VPA as an adjuvant therapy for GBM.

title: Accuracy of soft tissue profile predictions using WebCeph and Dolphin software in non-growing skeletal Class II cases treated with upper premolar extractions: A retrospective comparative study.
abstract: Introduction Aesthetic outcomes are a primary concern for adult orthodontic patients. Clinicians often rely on soft tissue simulation software, such as Dolphin Imaging (D-Tech) and WebCeph (D-Tech), to manage patient expectations. This study aimed to compare the accuracy of these two tools in predicting soft tissue profile changes in non-growing skeletal Class II patients treated with maxillary first premolar extractions. Methods A retrospective comparative study was conducted on patients treated by the same practitioner with bilateral maxillary first premolar extractions and maximum anchorage. From a private-practice database of 2535 patients treated between January 2015 and January 2025, 34 met the inclusion criteria after eligibility screening. Pre- and post-treatment lateral cephalometric radiographs and profile photographs were used to generate simulations. Predicted cephalometric measurements from D-Tech and W-Tech were compared with each other and with the actual post-treatment results. Statistical analyses included paired t-tests, one-sample t-tests, Bland-Altman plots, and linear regression. Results Thirty-four patients (10 males, 24 females; 35.7±3.5 years) were analysed. Both tools showed a significant discrepancy in the nasolabial angle versus actual results (P<0.001). D-Tech differed significantly in the subnasale to Holdaway-line distance (mean difference 0.81mm [95% CI 0.03 to 1.60]; P=0.042), while W-Tech differed in upper and lower lip position relative to the True Vertical Line (LL-TVL P=0.004; UL-TVL P=0.006). For the remaining parameters, both tools showed good agreement; D-Tech showed a proportional bias for lip-TVL position (greater underestimation at larger values), whereas W-Tech overestimated lower lip thickness. Conclusion Both Dolphin Imaging and WebCeph provide clinically applicable predictions for most soft tissue parameters. Several statistically significant lip-position discrepancies were within the range generally considered clinically imperceptible (=1.5-2.0mm), whereas the nasolabial angle showed a discrepancy that is both statistically and clinically relevant. Predictions should therefore be interpreted with caution, particularly for parameters prone to systematic bias.

title: Baseline MRI markers and clinical outcomes during anti-amyloid β therapy: A real-world study in a Japanese dementia center.
abstract: Importance Predictors of decline and of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) during anti-amyloid β therapy in routine care are undefined. Objective To identify baseline predictors of cognitive, functional, and safety outcomes. Design, setting, and participants Retrospective cohort of 161 consecutive patients initiating anti-amyloid β therapy at a Tokyo dementia center, 2024 to 2026 (lecanemab, 89; donanemab, 72). Exposures Lecanemab or donanemab. Main outcomes and measures Change in MMSE and CDR-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB); baseline medial temporal atrophy (VSRAD Z score), amyloid PET burden, and microbleeds; ARIA. Results With lecanemab, MMSE and CDR-SB declined significantly at every assessment (CDR-SB +0.79, +1.10, +1.60 at 6, 12, 18 months); memory and orientation declined while language was preserved. Greater baseline medial temporal atrophy was associated with greater 12-month CDR-SB worsening (r = 0.39; P = .01; n = 40); patients in the most severe standard category (Z ≥ 3) worsened by 2.62 versus 0.64 points (adjusted β = +2.18; P < .001). Atrophy was associated with older age (r = 0.19; P = .03) and with baseline memory-related measures - ADAS-Cog score (r = 0.32; P < .001) and the MMSE subdomains of delayed recall (β = -0.25; P = .006) and time orientation (β = -0.30; P = .04) - but not MMSE total score. Amyloid PET burden showed no significant association at most time points. All ARIA events were asymptomatic; ARIA-H occurred in 6 of 25 with microbleeds versus 3 of 136 without (odds ratio, 14.0; P < .001). Donanemab follow-up was 6 months. Conclusions and relevance Baseline medial temporal atrophy was associated with functional decline and microbleeds with ARIA-H. Pretreatment MRI may provide prognostic and safety information during anti-amyloid β therapy.

title: Rapid Progression of Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy With Sudden Cardiac Death Within the First Year of Heart Transplantation: A Case Report.
abstract: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is a major cause of mortality and morbidity within the first 3 years of heart transplantation (HT). CAV results in progressive coronary artery stenosis and may lead to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. In some cases, sudden cardiac death represents the initial presentation of CAV, as cardiac denervation blunts anginal symptoms that otherwise could have preceded sudden cardiac death (SCD). Here, we describe the case of a 56-year-old man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. He underwent left ventricular assist device implantation followed by orthotopic HT. Five months after transplantation, he presented with atypical mid-sternal chest discomfort initially thought to be musculoskeletal in origin. Routine coronary angiography at 12 months revealed severe, diffuse 3-vessel disease consistent with International Society of Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) CAV-3, and cardiac MRI revealed full thickness delayed enhancement in the inferior wall consistent with infarction. Despite overall preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) with an appropriate shock from a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) and was transferred with an intra-aortic balloon pump to a larger transplant center and underwent another heart transplantation. This case highlights rapid CAV progression leading to infarction and arrhythmia despite preserved LVEF, emphasizing the need for enhanced screening with biomarkers and imaging as well as earlier consideration for device-based strategies to prevent sudden cardiac death in high-risk transplant recipients.

title: Differentiating disseminated cryptococcosis from pulmonary cryptococcosis: Roles of clinical characteristics and cryptococcal antigen.
abstract: Abstract Distinguishing disseminated cryptococcosis (DC) from localized pulmonary cryptococcosis (PC) is crucial due to divergent management and disparate prognoses. This study aimed to recognize associated factors for DC from PC in non-human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) patients. Accordingly, 475 pathologically confirmed cryptococcosis cases (391 PC and 84 DC) were retrospectively reviewed over a 20-year period at a tertiary hospital in China. Clinical, radiographic, dynamic serum cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) titer profiles, treatment and prognosis were analyzed. Patients with DC were significantly associated with a history of glucocorticoid therapy (16.7% vs. 5.6%; P = 0.001) and autoimmune diseases (16.7% vs. 6.1%; P = 0.001) compared with PC, aggressive thoracic computed tomography findings, including patchy exudation ( P = 0.001) and cavitation ( P = 0.009), and markedly higher baseline median serum CrAg titers (1:1280 vs. 1:80, P < 0.001). By multivariable analysis, CNS symptoms (adjusted OR [aOR] 131.12, 95% CI 10.21-1683.9, P = 0.001), chronic liver disease (aOR 15.21, 95% CI 1.06-217.69, P = 0.045), and baseline serum CrAg ≥1:80 (aOR 13.51, 95% CI 1.39-131.07, P = 0.025) remained independently associated with DC. An initial CrAg titer ≥ 1:80 should prompt careful CNS evaluation and consideration of lumbar puncture. Patients with DC had significantly longer median CrAg clearance ( P = 0.001) and antifungal duration (18 vs. 6 months), with higher mortality (9.5% vs. 1.0%; P < 0.001) compared to PC. Early risk-stratification is imperative to optimize interventions and improve survival.

By multivariable analysis, CNS symptoms (adjusted OR [aOR] 131.12, 95% CI 10.21-1683.9, P = 0.001), chronic liver disease (aOR 15.21, 95% CI 1.06-217.69, P = 0.045), and baseline serum CrAg ≥1:80 (aOR 13.51, 95% CI 1.39-131.07, P = 0.025) remained independently associated with DC. An initial CrAg titer ≥ 1:80 should prompt careful CNS evaluation and consideration of lumbar puncture. Patients with DC had significantly longer median CrAg clearance (P = 0.001) and antifungal duration (18 vs. 6 months), with higher mortality (9.5% vs. 1.0%; P < 0.001) compared to PC. Early risk-stratification is imperative to optimize interventions and improve survival.

title: Pyogenic Sacroiliitis in Older Adults Presenting With Massive Retroperitoneal Abscess: A Case Report.
abstract: Pyogenic sacroiliitis (PSI) is an uncommon form of septic arthritis and is frequently diagnosed late in older adults because initial symptoms are nonspecific and imaging findings may be misattributed to other sources of infection. We report two older patients with PSI complicated by massive retroperitoneal and gluteal abscesses, highlighting the importance of early recognition and, when indicated, timely surgical source control. Case 1 was an 83-year-old woman in whom a conspicuous retroperitoneal abscess and abnormal urinalysis led to suspicion of an intra-abdominal or urinary tract source, delaying recognition of PSI. Despite antibiotics, she deteriorated with organ dysfunction; re-evaluation of the initial magnetic resonance imaging MRI identified the sacroiliac joint as the primary focus, and staged surgical drainage procedures were required, followed by a prolonged recovery. Case 2 was a 70-year-old woman who presented in septic shock after failing outpatient treatment for presumed lumbar spine disease. Based on the diagnostic pitfalls in Case 1, PSI was immediately suspected; emergency drainage of both retroperitoneal and gluteal collections was performed on the day of presentation, which was followed by rapid stabilization and recovery. These cases emphasize that, in older patients with low back or gluteal pain, the concurrent presence of retroperitoneal and gluteal abscesses should prompt careful evaluation of the sacroiliac joint. These observations suggest that early diagnosis and timely assessment for surgical source control may contribute to favorable outcomes in severe cases.

title: Coil Embolization and Open Splenectomy for a Massive Splenic Vein Aneurysm: A Case Report.
abstract: Background Splenic vein aneurysms (SVAs) are a rare vascular anomaly of the portal system that are often asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging. Intervention is reserved for aneurysms that are enlarging, thrombosed, symptomatic, or ruptured to avoid catastrophic complications. This can range from endovascular to open, complex procedures. Here, we present the case of a massive, symptomatic, partially thrombosed SVA that required a hybrid approach involving both minimally invasive and open surgery. Case presentation A 56-year-old woman presented to the emergency department for an infected right foot wound and was admitted for intravenous antibiotics and surgical debridement. While hospitalized, she had a worsening transaminitis with associated abdominal pain, prompting investigation with a computed tomography (CT) scan, which identified a massively dilated, partially thrombosed SVA measuring 18 cm. Given the enormous size of the aneurysm and substantial risk of impending rupture, urgent surgical intervention was planned. Preoperative coil embolization of the splenic artery was performed first to reduce the arterial inflow to the SVA and to minimize the risk of intraoperative hemorrhage during open resection. Three days after embolization, the patient underwent open splenectomy with aneurysmectomy for definitive management. The patient's postoperative course was complicated by a bleeding gastric ulcer that was successfully cauterized, and she was discharged home on postoperative Day 10 after receiving the recommended postsplenectomy vaccines. Conclusion No standard treatment algorithm exists for SVAs, as management is individualized, and treatment evidence is limited to case reports and series. This patient had one of the largest SVAs ever recorded, and management was based on the acuity of symptoms, size, and rupture risk of the aneurysm sac. This case also demonstrated the success of a novel management approach to massive SVAs, using preoperative embolization of the splenic artery followed by open resection without portal reconstruction.

title: Intravitreal methotrexate as a prophylactic strategy for proliferative vitreoretinopathy in high-risk retinal detachment.
abstract: Background Proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) remains the major cause of surgical failure in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD). This study evaluates the anatomical and functional outcomes, as well as the safety, of a standardized intraoperative intravitreal methotrexate infusion protocol during pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) in eyes with early stage PVR (grade B) or with advanced PVR (grade C). Methods A retrospective case series was conducted on 60 consecutive eyes of 59 patients with RRD and PVR grade B (n = 29) or grade C (n = 31) undergoing PPV with adjunct intraoperative methotrexate between November 2024 and February 2026 at a German tertiary center. Methotrexate 40 mg was administered via a 500 mL balanced salt solution infusion. Functional and structural testing included best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), intraocular pressure, multifocal electroretinogram, perimetry, and spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. The primary outcome measure was single-surgery anatomical success (SSAS) at 12 weeks after primary surgery or after silicone oil removal. Secondary outcomes included BCVA changes and complication rates. Results SSAS was achieved in 81.7% of all eyes, with a significantly higher success rate in eyes with PVR grade B compared to PVR grade C (93.1% versus 71.0%; p = 0.043). At 12 weeks, BCVA improved significantly in macula-off cases (p < 0.001) and remained stable in macula-on cases. In an exploratory subset of 17 patients postoperative multifocal electroretinogram and perimetry demonstrated preserved central retinal function. No ocular or systemic adverse events related to methotrexate occurred. Conclusions The standardized intraoperative intravitreal methotrexate infusion protocol was safe, feasible, and associated with high single-surgery reattachment rates, particularly in PVR grade B eyes. Anatomical outcomes in PVR grade C eyes were comparable to other complex PVR cohorts, without any drug-related local or systemic toxicity. Trial registration Not applicable (retrospective observational study).

title: Growth hormone-releasing hormone-secreting giant pheochromocytoma causing acromegaly: a case report with a review of the literature.
abstract: The ectopic secretion of growth hormone (GH) or growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) is responsible for fewer than 1% of acromegaly cases. Furthermore, within this small population, GHRH-secreting pheochromocytomas/paragangliomas (PPGLs) are even rarer. A 57-year-old Japanese woman presented to our hospital for treatment of a large left-sided pheochromocytoma (PCC). A physical examination revealed enlargement of the nose and lips as well as macroglossia, thereby raising the suspicion of acromegaly, which was biochemically confirmed by a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a slightly enlarged pituitary gland but no definitive tumor. A left adrenalectomy was performed after careful dose titration of doxazosin and metyrosine. Postoperative biochemical improvement of GH excess and immunohistochemical analysis of the resected tumor confirmed the diagnosis of GHRH-secreting PCC. Given the possibility that PPGLs produce various ectopic hormones and peptides, thorough physical examinations remain fundamental for the accurate diagnosis and optimal management of patients with these tumors.

title: Confluence Stones at the Junction of the Cystic Duct and an Aberrant Anterior Sectoral Bile Duct: A Case Report.
abstract: Confluence stones usually arise when gallstones impacted in the cystic duct migrate toward the biliary confluence. Surgical treatment can be technically demanding because of chronic inflammation and distorted anatomy. Confluence stones at the junction between the cystic duct and an aberrant bile duct are extremely rare. We report a successfully treated case of confluence stones arising at the junction of the cystic duct and an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct with a communicating accessory bile duct. A 38-year-old woman presented with abdominal pain, and biliary stones were detected. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct draining independently into the common bile duct. Biliary stones were identified both within this duct and at its junction with the cystic duct. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography confirmed the biliary anatomy and additionally revealed a communicating accessory bile duct between the anterior and posterior sectoral ducts. The stones within the distal portion of the aberrant duct were removed endoscopically, but the impacted confluence stones could not be extracted. Therefore, open surgery was performed. After exposure of the junction, the confluence stones were removed through a semicircumferential incision. Complete stone clearance was confirmed by intraoperative cholangioscopy and cholangiography. The patient was discharged on POD 11 with no bile leakage. At 14 months postoperatively, she remained asymptomatic and had experienced no episodes of cholangitis. We report a rare case of confluence stones arising at the junction of the cystic duct and an aberrant anterior sectoral bile duct. Preoperative assessment of the drainage territory and intraoperative evaluation of the duct diameter, ischemia, and tissue fragility are essential for appropriate and safe repair of the bile duct defect. The repair strategy should not rely on presumed bypass flow through a communicating accessory bile duct because its functional capacity cannot be reliably predicted.

title: Phyllodes Tumors of the Breast in 2026: A Contemporary Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Surgical Margins, Prognosis, and Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Phyllodes tumors of the breast are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms characterized by significant heterogeneity regarding morphology, biological behavior, and clinical outcome. This review summarizes current developments in the diagnosis, histopathological and molecular classification, therapeutic management, and emerging technologies associated with phyllodes tumors of the breast. A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar, focusing on publications from the 2000-2026 period. The literature search covered publications from January 1, 2000, to September 30, 2026, and was last updated on September 30, 2026. Mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging contribute to preoperative assessment, although significant diagnostic overlap with fibroadenomas persists. Core needle biopsy is a key diagnostic tool, yet lesion heterogeneity can limit the accuracy of histological classification. Advances in molecular pathology have identified mutations and pathways associated with the progression and aggressiveness of phyllodes tumors, though these have not yet replaced morphological assessment. Surgical excision with negative margins remains the primary therapeutic approach, while the risk of local recurrence depends on histological grade, surgical margins, and other clinicopathological characteristics. Radiotherapy in phyllodes tumors of the breast appears to offer benefits primarily regarding local control in selected high-risk cases. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, radiomics, and digital pathology, are proving to be promising tools for diagnosis, grading, and prognostic assessment. Overall, modern management of phyllodes tumors of the breast is shifting toward more personalized and multifactorial approaches.

title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
abstract: MRI field-strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low-field scanners with the image quality of high-field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations, as uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions insufficiently examined and scarce paired data limit their learning of how tissue contrast and anatomical visibility change across field strengths. To address these challenges, we propose UniField++, a two-agent framework that unifies enhancement tasks across multiple field-strength transitions, including 64mT-to-3T and 3T-to-7T. Unified learning allows both the VLM-based planner and the flow-matching-based enhancer to draw on field-dependent image characteristics observed across tasks, rather than relying on a single transition. Trained with radiologists' annotations of hallucination-prone regions and corresponding correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow-matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high-risk regions for additional refinement. Together, cross-transition learning and risk-guided refinement support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole-brain segmentation Macro Dice by an average of 0.1457 over the original low-field images. Code is available at https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/UniField_plusplus.

title: Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning with Visual Hierarchy for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
abstract: Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to detect anomalies in previously unseen classes using auxiliary images, with applications such as industrial visual inspection and medical imaging. Recent vision-language-model-based approaches improve ZSAD by aligning textual and visual representations, while distributional prompting further models prompt variability for unseen categories. However, existing methods do not explicitly combine normality-referenced distributional modeling with hierarchy-specific prompt specialization, limiting their ability to model anomalous semantics relative to normality while addressing both image-level detection and fine-grained localization. We propose Hierarchical Knowledge-Guided Distributional Prompt Learning (HiDist), a normality-referenced hierarchical distributional prompt framework for ZSAD. HiDist models each prompt token with a diagonal Gaussian distribution and generates stochastic prompt variations through Monte Carlo sampling. Rather than learning normal and anomalous distributions independently, anomalous prompt distributions are parameterized as deviations from learned normal references, explicitly encoding their dependency. The resulting distributions are specialized into global and local representations for image-level detection and pixel-level localization, respectively, while an adapted global visual representation guides hierarchical alignment. Experiments on seven industrial and medical datasets demonstrate strong cross-dataset performance across anomaly detection and localization tasks. Extensive ablation and representation analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed distributional modeling and hierarchy-specific representation learning.

title: Data-Efficient Classifier Pretraining Through Diffusion Models
abstract: Machine learning with limited data is susceptible to overfitting, especially with modern deep neural networks. Prior to the introduction of AlexNet, reconstruction-based pretraining with auto-encoder and denoising auto-encoder were found to be beneficial, partially due to the limited size of the training sets at the time. Motivated by these traditional approaches, we propose DiffPT, a simple diffusion modeling approach to pretrain a given classifier backbone for limited domain-specific training data. We experiment on time-series data, standard natural-image benchmarks, and medical imaging datasets, and contrast the diffusion approach to a multitude of modern and traditional un/self-supervised methods. While contrastive pretraining performs better on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet in low-data regimes, DiffPT is particularly effective on medical imaging and time-series tasks, where it outperforms self-supervised baselines across a range of low-data regimes. Our results suggest that DiffPT is a simple and effective approach for data-efficient classifier pretraining on different modalities.

title: TAN: A Size- and Form-Adaptive Masked-Convolution Encoder for Tissue Graphs
abstract: Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.

title: From Adult Renal Masses to Pediatric Wilms Tumors: Evaluating Cross-Domain Generalization of Kidney Lesion Segmentation on MRI
abstract: Deep learning segmentation models for pediatric oncology are often trained on small, single-center cohorts, whereas much larger datasets exist for adult diseases, such as kidney cancer. Whether models trained on adult renal lesions generalize to pediatric Wilms tumors remains unclear. We trained a segmentation model on single-sequence T1- or T2-weighted adult kidney MRI and evaluated it on a held-out adult test set and a pediatric Wilms tumor cohort, where it was compared with a pediatric-specific nnU-Net. Segmentation performance was quantified using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance. On the adult test set, the model achieved a median DSC of 0.86 for renal lesions. On the pediatric cohort, the adult-trained model achieved a median DSC of 0.85 compared with 0.90 for the pediatric-specific model. Despite differences in age, anatomy, and tumor type, the adult-trained model showed promising performance on pediatric Wilms tumors, with only a modest difference in median DSC compared with the pediatric-specific model. However, non-inferiority could not be shown, highlighting the value of pediatric training data. In future work, a fine-tuning strategy could be explored.

title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.

title: Beyond Multi-Stage Pipelines: A Label-Correlation Ensemble for Multi-Label Retinal Fundus Disease Classification
abstract: Retinal fundus images frequently carry more than one disease, and public fundus datasets are heterogeneous and severely long-tailed. Clinical triage suggests a staged design, in which a screening gate, a disease-group router and group-specific classifiers operate in sequence, but it is unclear whether this hierarchy earns its complexity. We present a controlled comparison of three architectures on a unified 39-target label space built from RFMiD 1.0, RFMiD 2.0 and ODIR-5K (12,652 images): (i) a three-stage gated cascade of eight models, (ii) a flat model with 39 independent sigmoid outputs, and (iii) a label-correlation model that replaces the flat linear head with 39 learned label queries and a two-layer transformer decoder. All three share one Swin-V2-B backbone, one preprocessing pipeline and one training protocol, so differences are attributable to the architecture. Staging offers no consistent advantage: tracing every missed disease instance to the stage that lost it shows that the two coarse gates discard 34.2% of true instances while the fine-grained classifiers lose only 6.7%, and the gates' hard zeros depress the cascade's macro-AUC to 0.747. Label-correlation modeling gives the largest single gain, raising the detection rate from 0.621 to 0.682 (0.689 with test-time augmentation). Blending the flat and label-correlation models under four-view test-time augmentation is the best configuration on six of eight metrics (exact match 0.694, micro-F1 0.678, macro-F1 0.456, macro-AUC 0.972). On definition-matched class subsets it matches or exceeds four recent studies on macro- and micro-F1, most clearly on low-support pathologies. We also show that ensembling a gated cascade with continuous-output models is harmful, and that per-source negative sampling is needed to remove a dataset shortcut that otherwise yields a spurious AUC of 1.000.

title: DinoMUSE: A DINOv2-guided Framework for Unsupervised Lateral Motion Estimation in Ultrasound Elastography
abstract: Quasi-static ultrasound elastography (USE) is a non-invasive imaging method for assessing soft tissue mechanical properties. Limited by low resolution, low sampling frequency and lack of phase information in the lateral direction, accurate lateral motion estimation remains a critical bottleneck in USE. Existing methods mainly rely on local image matching and physical constraints (such as tissue incompressibility assumption and effective Poisson's ratio), which lack sufficient contextual information. We present DinoMUSE, a DINO-guided mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework for unsupervised lateral motion estimation in USE. DinoMUSE incorporates high-level visual representations learned by DINOv2 into the motion estimation network to provide global contextual guidance. To facilitate effective interaction between DINOv2 features and local matching features, an MoE-based feature-fusion module adaptively transforms and integrates the two representations. Evaluations against NCC, GLUE, RAFT, and sPICTURE on simulation and in-vivo breast datasets show that DinoMUSE substantially improves lateral estimation accuracy while maintaining competitive axial performance. Specifically, DinoMUSE reduces the mean square error (MSE) of lateral displacement and strain estimation by 60% and 65%, respectively, compared with a SOTA algorithm on the simulation dataset. For in-vivo breast data, DinoMUSE achieves axial strain SNR and CNR of 5.70 and 4.82, and lateral strain SNR and CNR of 4.61 and 2.23, compared to 4.11 and 3.32, and 4.57 and 2.13 for the best competing method, alongside improved lesion visualization. These findings indicate the potential of leveraging transferable visual representations and adaptive feature fusion to improve lateral motion estimation in USE. The code is available at xxxxxxxx.

title: Implicit Neural Models for Direct Multi-Shell Diffusion MRI Signal Estimation
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging is a noninvasive technique that is sensitive to the motion of water molecules in human tissue. The image signal is commonly described in q-space; however, a complete coverage of this space is often infeasible due to hardware and acquisition time limitations. In this work, we propose to represent the entire diffusion signal using an implicit neural representation network with wavelet activation functions. The signal space is encoded using Fourier features and spherical harmonics basis functions for a continuous output distribution of the raw diffusion data, enabling both super-resolution and q-space interpolation. Additionally, we introduce a pretraining strategy using a group template, enabling faster per-subject optimisation when combined with nonlinear registrations of subjects into template space. We tested the method with 10 subjects from the Human Connectome Project and 26 subjects from in-house data (multidimensional diffusion MRI from a Parkinson's disease cohort). The results show that the proposed method yields high-fidelity reconstructions with significantly reduced memory requirements compared to raw diffusion-weighted images. The pretraining scheme showed good generalisability properties on data acquired with very different protocols. We further assess the method on downstream metrics relevant to diffusion MRI data from the learned representations.

title: Benchmarking and Improvement of Artifact Segmentation Methods in H&E-Stained Whole Slide Imaging
abstract: Technical artifacts introduced during tissue preparation or slide scanning remain a major obstacle to developing robust computational pathology algorithms for hematoxylin and eosin (HE)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs). Despite the growing number of quality-control tools, their real-world utility remains hard to assess because of the limited number of publicly available implementations and the lack of systematic, multi-dataset comparisons. This paper presents a benchmark of artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs. After a literature review, six publicly available algorithms were selected and compared in terms of their ability to segment artifact-free tissue and selected artifact classes. Two publicly available datasets and a newly introduced dataset released to support further research were used for evaluation. Tissue samples from multiple medical centers and different organs are included, enabling evaluation across heterogeneous data sources. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice Index, pixel-level recall, and false discovery rate for artifact-free tissue segmentation. For algorithms supporting multiclass artifact segmentation, class-wise Dice Index and inter-class misclassification were evaluated. In addition to segmentation quality, processing time was assessed. Statistical analysis revealed significant differences in segmentation performance between methods. HistoKit, which incorporates a modified version of the GrandQC, was identified as the best-performing algorithm, while HistoQC was the worst. In terms of artifact types, dark spots and out of focus regions were harder to segment than others. Finally, a simple post-processing step was introduced for HistoKit, which further improved segmentation performance. The benchmark establishes a reference for evaluating and developing artifact segmentation methods for HE-stained WSIs.

title: GliomaINK: A Tumor and Anatomy Conditioned Flow Matching Framework for 3D MRI Sequence Synthesis in Glioma Patients
abstract: Background: Incomplete multiparametric MR examinations limit glioma characterization and downstream AI tools. Generative models can synthesize missing MRI sequences, but anatomical structure and clinically relevant tumor features are challenging to preserve. We propose GliomaINK, an anatomy-guided conditional flow matching framework for cross-sequence 3D brain MRI synthesis. Methods: A 3D SwinUNETR predicted the conditional velocity field while an auxiliary topology-preserving loss encouraged structural consistency. The model was trained on 1,083 patients from the BraTS-AG dataset and independently tested on an in-house clinical cohort. Downstream tasks include image quality, tumor segmentation, IDH1 mutation-status prediction, and overall survival prediction. Two radiologists independently evaluated the anatomical fidelity, pathological representation, and overall image quality of the synthesized images. Results: GliomaINK exhibited the highest PSNR across all six MRI translation directions in both evaluation cohorts. In the BraTS-AG test set, the PSNR reached $25.64\pm0.55$ dB for the T2W-to-T1C synthesis, compared with $13.78\pm0.32$ dB for Pix2Pix and $18.90\pm0.53$ dB for SPADE. For downstream tumor segmentation, the method showed strong performance across tumor subregions with Dice scores reaching $0.928\pm0.014$ for edema, and $0.885\pm0.040$ for enhancing tumor. For the IDH1 mutation-status prediction, GliomaINK achieved the highest AUROC score in four of the six sequence configurations, reaching $0.827\pm0.088$. Conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis demonstrating potential for preservation of clinically relevant information in synthesized MRI and improving downstream tasks.

Two radiologists independently evaluated the anatomical fidelity, pathological representation, and overall image quality of the synthesized images.
  Results: GliomaINK exhibited the highest PSNR across all six MRI translation directions in both evaluation cohorts. In the BraTS-AG test set, the PSNR reached $25.64\pm0.55$ dB for the T2W-to-T1C synthesis, compared with $13.78\pm0.32$ dB for Pix2Pix and $18.90\pm0.53$ dB for SPADE. For downstream tumor segmentation, the method showed strong performance across tumor subregions with Dice scores reaching $0.928\pm0.014$ for edema, and $0.885\pm0.040$ for enhancing tumor. For the IDH1 mutation-status prediction, GliomaINK achieved the highest AUROC score in four of the six sequence configurations, reaching $0.827\pm0.088$.
  Conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis demonstrating potential for preservation of clinically relevant information in synthesized MRI and improving downstream tasks.

title: LUMINR: Intensity-conditioned Meta-learned INRs for Accelerated Medical Image Registration
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have been applied to deformable image registration, where a lightweight network maps a spatial coordinate to a deformation vector. Because an INR encodes one specific signal in its parameters, a fresh network must be optimized for every image pair at test time, which is slow. Existing methods reduce this cost by meta-learning an initialization across a population of image pairs, and condition the weights of the INR globally, so the same conditioning applies at every coordinate while the deformation field it initializes varies across the domain. We propose LUMINR, a meta-learning framework that accelerates this per-pair fitting and in which the conditioning is local instead. LUMINR uses an INR that maps a coordinate, together with local intensity and gradient features, to a deformation vector, so the conditioning varies over the domain at the resolution of the field being modelled. Its objective is to find an initialization of the INR parameters from which the network can be fine-tuned to register any unseen pair in only a few optimization iterations. We evaluate LUMINR on 3D deformable registration of brain MRI from the OASIS dataset, where local conditioning and the meta-learned initialization prove complementary: early in fitting they reach a markedly higher accuracy than either does alone. Fine-tuned from that initialization, LUMINR matches the accuracy of the same conditioned INR fit from scratch in roughly a tenth of the gradient steps and a tenth of the wall-clock time, while the deformation fields stay smooth with negligible folding.

title: NV-Generate-Body: 3D Latent Diffusion Model forControllable Anatomy, Tumor, and Demographic Body Mask Synthesis
abstract: Curating large labeled CT datasets is expensive and constrained by patient privacy. We present NV-Generate-BodyMask, a 3D latent diffusion model that synthesizes whole-body CT segmentation masks with precise, joint control over organ anatomy, tumor burden, and patient demographics. The model operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen mask autoencoder, generating $256^3$ volumetric label maps conditioned on a 19-dimensional vector via Adaptive Group Normalization and cross-attention. A size-adaptive ROI loss with spatial halo weighting and a paired tumor injection pipeline enable accurate tumor size conditioning despite the scarcity of annotated tumor cases. Trained on 8,571 masks across 26 cohorts spanning 132 labels, the model achieves Spearman $ρ= 0.70$--$0.92$ for organ size, 85--100\% tumor recall for lung, pancreatic, colon, and bone lesions, and strong demographic alignment (BMI $ρ= 0.78$, sex-conditioned perfect prostate control).

title: Landmark-Free and Scale-Blind Multi-View Registration of Preoperative Liver Models to Intraoperative Surfaces
abstract: Augmented-reality guidance in laparoscopic liver resection requires aligning preoperative 3D liver models from CT/MRI with intraoperative surfaces. Monocular reconstruction in most cases cannot guarantee scale, albeit rigid-motion registration requires scale as an input. Our proposed framework ``SimCompose'' estimates the full similarity transformation $\Sim$, including scale, without relying on landmarks and applies the same transformation across multiple views with known relative geometry. However, reliable detection of registration failures remains challenging in surgical settings, where ground-truth alignment is generally unavailable. For this, we propose a geometry-based selector that evaluates candidate transformations without requiring ground truth. Large disagreement among these transformations is used to flag potentially unreliable registrations. Finally, we propose to use a non-rigid refinement based on a low-dimensional deformation model from Neo-Hookean simulations in the Simulation Open Framework Architecture (SOFA), without additional network training. SimCompose is trained exclusively on synthetic partial views. Its encoder processes point clouds normalised to a unit root-mean-square radius, without access to metric scale, and filters each view before multi-view fusion. Evaluation on unseen synthetic data (300 single-view pairs per run; 100 three-view registrations) shows that multi-view integration and candidate selection increase the success rate under stringent $\Sim$ accuracy criteria from 38.4% for a single-view, single-method configuration to 77%. Existing learning-based baselines do not satisfy these criteria even when provided with the exact scale. On five in-vivo patients with 92 keyframes, the rigid registration stage reduces surface error more than three-fold relative to learning-based baselines with external scale information.

title: Enzyme-Activatable Probe for Tumor Bimodal Imaging, Intraoperative Navigation, and Urinalysis.
abstract: We develope an enzyme-activatable platform (NO 2 -RGD-Gd) for the integrated urinary biomarker detection, highcontrast fluorescence-magnetic resonance (MR) dualmodal imaging, and real-time image-guided surgical navigation within a single molecule. The advantages, including the favorable tumor-targeting affinity (RGD peptide), high renal clearance efficiency, and tumor-specific fluorescence activation, are achieved by rationally engineering the molecular architecture. Benefiting from these characteristics, the NO 2 -RGD-Gd effectively bridges the boundary between diagnosis and therapy, achieving outstanding combinatorial performance in in vivo applications. It allows early and precise diagnosis through urinary biomarkers, provides anatomical-pathological and molecular imaging information of tumor lesions via fluorescence-MR dual-modal imaging, and delineates tumor boundaries for accurate surgical navigation relying on tumor-targeted activatable fluorescence imaging signals. Furthermore, all these processes can be realized simply via intravenous injection, offering a more efficient and feasible strategy for integrated diagnostic and therapeutic applications.

title: Ocular morphology and morphometry of the great egret (Ardea alba): A comprehensive anatomical description.
abstract: Ardea alba (Linnaeus, 1758) is widely distributed, yet knowledge of its ocular morphology remains limited. This study described the morphometry and morphology of the eyeball and its accessory glands in six specimens using radiography, morphometry, light and scanning electron microscopy, and 3D scanning. The eyeballs showed similar descriptive morphometric values in the right and left eyes, accounting for approximately 11.2% of head mass and 12.12% of total skull length. The eye was classified as the flat type, a morphology previously associated in the literature with diurnal birds, featuring a yellow iris and a circular pupil. The scleral ring consists of 14 bilateral type A ossicles associated with hyaline scleral cartilage. Histologically, the cornea showed a well-defined Bowman's membrane, and the retina had 10 distinct layers. The pleated type pecten emerged from the optic nerve and extended toward the vitreous body. The accessory glands were characterized as follows: the Harderian gland (type II) was the most developed; the lacrimal gland was "hockey-stick" shaped; and the nasal gland (salt gland) was supraorbital in location and pyramidal in appearance. These results provide a robust anatomical basis for comparative avian ophthalmology.
