title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
abstract: Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation does not significantly improve cross-population generalization. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not translate into better performance on pediatric data.

title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.

title: FPG-Seg: Annotation-free Retinal Vessel Topology Segmentation
abstract: State-of-the art approaches to retinal vessel segmentation typically require extensive annotations, a highly time-consuming process, reliant on clinical expertise. We present FPG-Seg, an annotation-free pipeline for retinal vessel segmentation combining classical vesselness filtering, Bayesian deep learning and topology-aware graph reconstruction to segment retinal vessel topology without manual labels. Tested across four widely used benchmark datasets for retinal vessel segmentation, FPG-Seg attains a clDice of $0.74{-}0.78$, representing $86{-}98\%$ of the performance of an equivalent fully-supervised baseline, despite using no manual annotations for training or hyperparameter tuning. As part of this work, we also provide, to our knowledge, the first performance benchmark of an annotation-free vessel segmentation method on FIVES.

title: CRUX: Clinical-Text Anchoring for Cross-Institutional CT-Pathology Fusion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
abstract: Accurate prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) benefits from integrating computed tomography (CT) and histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), which capture complementary macroscopic and microscopic disease characteristics. Fusing these modalities is difficult: their features come from different pretrained foundation-model encoders and lack spatial correspondence, and both are sensitive to institution-specific acquisition and staining, causing multimodal models to overfit site-specific artifacts and generalize poorly. We present CRUX (CRoss-modal Unification via teXt anchoring), a fusion framework that uses clinical text---encoded by a biomedical language model---as an institution-invariant semantic anchor. Because clinical variables follow standardized classification systems, their embeddings occupy a representation space that is consistent across institutions, providing a stable reference frame for aligning heterogeneous imaging features. CRUX introduces a text-mediated cross-modal bridge in which CT- and pathology-derived text-query summaries exchange information within a compact text semantic space through a learnable hub token, avoiding direct image-space cross-attention that would propagate domain-specific artifacts. We evaluate on 2,157 NSCLC patients from five hospitals, holding out one hospital (N=446) entirely for external validation. CRUX attains an external concordance index (C-index) of 0.761, the highest among all unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal configurations. Notably, direct CT-WSI fusion degrades under distribution shift, whereas text anchoring restores and improves cross-institutional generalization. These results indicate that language-model-encoded clinical text is an effective structured prior for robust, generalizable multimodal cancer prognosis.

title: Really Need Recursion? Revisiting One-pass Registration with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance
abstract: Deformable image registration is a fundamental challenge in medical image analysis. Recent deep learning-based methods typically adopt either one-pass architectures that complete registration in a single network iteration, or recursive architectures that refine registration through multiple passes. While recursive methods often improve accuracy, they incur substantial computational overhead and slower inference speed. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of recursion for high-performance deformable registration and propose M2CG, a one-pass registration network with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance. It performs multi-step progressive pyramid registration within a single iteration, guided at each step by contextual cues from three levels (previous, current, and subsequent steps) and four spaces (image space, image feature space, segmentation space, and segmentation feature space). Our M2CG supports both unsupervised (without any labels) and semi-supervised (with segmentation labels for partial training data) registration, and has achieved state-of-the-art performance across two well-benchmarked inter-/intra-patient medical registration tasks with eight public datasets. Our findings suggest that the current reliance on recursion may stem from the absence of sufficient contextual cues that comprehensively characterize the remaining distance to the target alignment.

title: CF-NODE: Counterfactual Spatial Node Intervention for Test-Time Adaptation Under Domain Shift, Evaluated Across Five Diabetic Retinopathy Datasets
abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.

title: LGGS: Longitudinal MRI Reconstruction via Guided Group Sparsity
abstract: Serial MRI is routinely performed in current clinical practice for disease surveillance and applications such as MR-guided radiotherapy. However, long MRI scan times increase costs and limit patient access, making accelerated image reconstruction of broad clinical importance. Previous scans of the same patient contain image information highly correlated with the current exam, yet existing reconstruction methods rarely exploit this information. Major challenges in the effective use of prior scans include inter-visit misregistration, pathological changes, and image phase variation. In this work, we propose Longitudinal Guided Group Sparsity (LGGS), an interpretable deep-learning framework for longitudinally informed MRI reconstruction derived from classical group sparsity. The prior scan is incorporated into the reconstruction regularizer through learned phase-invariant circulant attention that identifies corresponding features across exams. This formulation provides robustness to local in-plane and through-plane misregistration as well as inter-visit phase variation. Across acceleration rates, LGGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on longitudinal T1-weighted multi-coil brain MRI data, outperforming the evaluated unguided and longitudinally informed reconstruction methods, with substantially fewer learned parameters. We further evaluated the contributions of multiple guide slices and phase-invariant similarity and demonstrated that accelerated prior images can also serve as effective guides with minimal degradation in reconstruction quality.

title: HilbertGen-3D:Hilbert--Multifractal Conditioning for Topology-Aware 3D Generation
abstract: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.

title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.

title: An Anatomy-Aware Staged Pipeline for Vessel-Specific Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation in CT and MR Angiography
abstract: The TopAneu 2026 challenge requires intracranial aneurysms to be segmented at the voxel level and assigned to one of more than fifty vessel-specific classes, on CT and MR angiography alike. We address it with a six-stage anatomy-aware pipeline rather than a single segmentation network. A logistic-regression classifier routes each scan to a modality-specific branch; networks segment the vasculature, first as a binary mask and then over the full 36-class arterial taxonomy; a candidate localiser turns raw angiography and vessel priors into suspicious regions; a candidate-centred network segments the lesion in each crop; connected components become instances; and a per-instance classifier assigns each its anatomical location. Two principles organise the design. Whenever an upstream model output becomes a downstream training input it is generated out-of-fold, so no stage trains on unrealistically clean predictions of itself. And the anatomical decision is made once per lesion rather than once per voxel, which fits the data: of 406 connected aneurysm components in the full release, 405 carry exactly one location label. Task 1 is read off the Task 2 mask, making the two consistent by construction. We report stage-wise performance and a five-part ablation isolating what vessel priors and class-aware sampling contribute at each stage.

title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.
abstract: Importance Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited. Objective To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries. Design, setting, and participants This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries. Main outcomes and measures The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined. Results Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians. Conclusions and relevance Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.

title: Neoadjuvant Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Before Inferior Vena Cava Thrombectomy for Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with inferior vena cava (IVC) tumor thrombus is associated with substantial perioperative risk and frequent recurrence despite nephrectomy and thrombectomy. No established neoadjuvant local therapy exists for this high-risk population. Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety, clinical outcomes, and exploratory biomarker effects of neoadjuvant stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) targeting IVC tumor thrombus before nephrectomy and thrombectomy. Design, setting, and participants This single-center prospective phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with newly diagnosed RCC and Mayo level II to IV IVC tumor thrombus eligible for neoadjuvant SABR and definitive surgery from July 2015 to January 2024. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to August 2026. Intervention Neoadjuvant SABR to the radiographically defined IVC tumor thrombus, delivered as 40 Gy in 5 fractions or 36 Gy in 3 fractions, followed by radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy. Main outcomes and measures The primary end point was 1-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) compared with a prespecified historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7%. Secondary outcomes included 90-day perioperative morbidity and mortality, adverse events, pulmonary embolism, overall survival, and cancer-specific survival. Exploratory analyses included Ki-67 immunohistochemistry and tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA. Results Of 23 patients who received neoadjuvant SABR, 22 completed surgery, and 21 were included in the primary RFS analysis. Of 21 included patients, 12 (57%) were male, and the median (IQR) age was 62.5 (54.0-73.2) years. A total of 19 patients had clear-cell RCC; all tumors were grade 3 or 4, and 3 patients had metastatic disease at enrollment. At a median (range) follow-up of 108.6 (2.0-127.2) months, 1-year RFS was 71.4% (80% CI, 56.6-82.0; 95% CI, 47.2-86.0), meeting the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion based on comparison with the historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7% (P = .09). One-year overall survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3) and cancer-specific survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3). No 90-day perioperative mortality occurred; 4 grade 4 treatment-attributed events occurred, but no grade 4/5 radiation-attributed toxic effects occurred. Ki-67 expression was reduced in patients with irradiated tumor thrombus compared with nonirradiated controls. Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA was detected in all patients with available plasma and declined after treatment. Conclusions and relevance In this nonrandomized clinical trial, neoadjuvant SABR before nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy appeared feasible with an acceptable safety profile. RFS met the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion but remains exploratory and warrants further evaluation. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02473536.

title: Primary Pure Yolk Sac Tumor of the Urinary Bladder: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Yolk sac tumors are malignant germ cell tumors that typically arise in the gonads. Although extragonadal cases have been reported, primary involvement of the urinary tract is extremely rare. Case presentation A 67-year-old man presented with gross hematuria. Cystoscopy and contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 6-cm bladder mass. Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings (alpha-fetoprotein, glypican-3, and Sal-like protein 4 positivity) were consistent with a yolk sac tumor without a urothelial carcinoma component. Additional examinations revealed no primary lesions elsewhere, leading to the diagnosis of a primary bladder yolk sac tumor. The patient received four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy and has remained recurrence-free for 2 years. Conclusions Patients with primary bladder yolk sac tumors, although rare, may achieve favorable outcomes with combined surgical resection and chemotherapy.
originalAbstract:
Introduction

Yolk sac tumors are malignant germ cell tumors that typically arise in the gonads. Although extragonadal cases have been reported, primary involvement of the urinary tract is extremely rare.

Case presentation

A 67-year-old man presented with gross hematuria. Cystoscopy and contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 6-cm bladder mass. Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings (alpha-fetoprotein, glypican-3, and Sal-like protein 4 positivity) were consistent with a yolk sac tumor without a urothelial carcinoma component. Additional examinations revealed no primary lesions elsewhere, leading to the diagnosis of a primary bladder yolk sac tumor. The patient received four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy and has remained recurrence-free for 2 years.

Conclusions

Patients with primary bladder yolk sac tumors, although rare, may achieve favorable outcomes with combined surgical resection and chemotherapy.

title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Response to the Correspondence Regarding "Cutaneous Metastasis From Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Eight Years After Initial Surgery".
abstract: We sincerely thank Dr. Sengul and colleagues for their insightful comments on our case report of skin metastasis in papillary thyroid cancer (PTC). They questioned the adequacy of local excision and suggested completion thyroidectomy to enable radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy or systemic therapy. We appreciate their perspective but explain our rationale, given the exceptional rarity of isolated cutaneous metastasis and limited evidence-based guidelines. Complete surgical excision may be appropriate for carefully selected patients with solitary cutaneous metastasis, whereas RAI or systemic therapy should be considered according to disease extent, iodine avidity, tumor biology, and patient-specific factors. We agree that TSH suppression alone does not explain the development of metastasis and that TERT promoter mutations may provide additional insight into the aggressive biological behavior of PTC. Despite the loss of thyroglobulin (Tg) expression in the metastasis, our multimodal surveillance-including ultrasonography and CT-has shown no recurrence, and we will offer functional imaging when clinical indicated. No evidence of recurrent or additional metastatic disease during follow-up, and per 2025 ATA guidelines, shared decision-making favored thyroid preservation with close follow-up. Future disease progression would prompt reconsideration of total thyroidectomy with RAI or targeted therapy.

title: [Enteral contrast media-when, what, and how?]
abstract: Background Enteral contrast media (CM) administration in abdominal computed tomography (CT) is handled inconsistently across Germany. Objective To present the current recommendations on enteral CM administration based on the key questions of when, what, and how, and to translate them into radiological practice. Materials and methods Synthesis of indication-based recommendations, CM classes and their technical properties, and the practical execution of both routes of administration, based on the German Radiological Society (DRG) recommendations, current guidelines, published evidence, and institutional practice. Results Positive oral CM are obsolete for most abdominal indications-including acute abdomen, ileus, and trauma-and are contraindicated when gastrointestinal bleeding or ischemia is suspected. In suspected perforation, routine oral contrast should be omitted and barium sulfate is contraindicated, whereas water-soluble iodinated agents remain an option when a leak has to be demonstrated specifically. Furthermore, enteral contrast with neutral oral CM remains useful for upper gastrointestinal tumor staging and enterography (preferably magnetic resonance enterography). Conclusion Indication-appropriate, guideline-based enteral contrast administration reduces unnecessary burden without compromising diagnostic accuracy and should be embedded in standardized workflows.
originalAbstract:
Background

Enteral contrast media (CM) administration in abdominal computed tomography (CT) is handled inconsistently across Germany.

Objective

To present the current recommendations on enteral CM administration based on the key questions of when, what, and how, and to translate them into radiological practice.

Materials and methods

Synthesis of indication-based recommendations, CM classes and their technical properties, and the practical execution of both routes of administration, based on the German Radiological Society (DRG) recommendations, current guidelines, published evidence, and institutional practice.

Results

Positive oral CM are obsolete for most abdominal indications-including acute abdomen, ileus, and trauma-and are contraindicated when gastrointestinal bleeding or ischemia is suspected. In suspected perforation, routine oral contrast should be omitted and barium sulfate is contraindicated, whereas water-soluble iodinated agents remain an option when a leak has to be demonstrated specifically. Furthermore, enteral contrast with neutral oral CM remains useful for upper gastrointestinal tumor staging and enterography (preferably magnetic resonance enterography).

Conclusion

Indication-appropriate, guideline-based enteral contrast administration reduces unnecessary burden without compromising diagnostic accuracy and should be embedded in standardized workflows.

title: IgG4-related disease of the pelvic floor musculature mimicking neoplasm: a case report with imaging-pathologic correlation.
abstract: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory condition that can form tumefactive mass-like lesions and mimic malignancy across organ systems. We describe a rare presentation involving the deep pelvic floor musculature with imaging-pathologic correlation while underscoring diagnostic pitfalls. A 49-year-old man with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, night sweats, and left lower quadrant abdominal pain underwent CT of the abdomen and pelvis, which demonstrated a right posterior pelvic sidewall mass and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Pelvic MRI demonstrated an ill-defined intramuscular mass centered in the right iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus muscles. Relative to skeletal muscle, the lesion demonstrated iso- to low T1 signal intensity, intermediate T2 signal intensity, restricted diffusion, and moderate, diffuse contrast enhancement, raising concern for neoplasm or an inflammatory process. Image-guided biopsy revealed fibrotic soft tissue with severe lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and increased IgG4-reactive plasma cells. The IgG4+/IgG+ plasma cell ratio was > 75%, consistent with IgG4-RD when integrated with the clinical, laboratory, imaging and pathologic findings. IgG4-related disease with mass-like involvement of the pelvic floor musculature has not, to the best of our knowledge, been previously reported in the English literature. This entity can present as an ill-defined, enhancing, diffusion-restricting intramuscular mass and therefore may mimic a neoplastic process.

title: AI-enhanced routine CT for opportunistic osteoporosis screening and risk assessment.
abstract: Osteoporosis-related fractures create a large and often preventable burden, yet many individuals undergoing CT for unrelated care do not receive skeletal assessment. This review evaluates artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled use of routine CT for opportunistic case-finding and risk assessment, with emphasis on the boundary between promising retrospective performance and safe clinical implementation. Automated vertebral segmentation and CT-derived bone-density estimation can reduce manual workload, and published diagnostic studies report high discrimination in selected cohorts. However, pooled estimates are heterogeneous because the reference standard, anatomical target, CT acquisition, reconstruction, contrast status, calibration method, prevalence, and validation design differ substantially across studies. These differences preclude a universal CT threshold or a universal minimum detector-row requirement; detector-row configuration should be considered together with the broader acquisition and reconstruction parameters. For implementation, AI should be deployed as a validated triage tool-not as a stand-alone diagnostic replacement for clinical assessment and indicated DXA/QCT. A credible pathway requires a defined CT-protocol eligibility check; pre-specified vertebral region of interest and exclusions; protocol- and contrast-aware quantification; scanner-specific quality assurance and calibration monitoring where applicable; external validation in representative populations; and an explicit route from an AI alert to confirmatory testing and treatment evaluation. AI may also enable concurrent vertebral-fracture and body-composition assessment, but clinical utility must be shown through downstream testing, treatment, fracture, workload, equity, and cost outcomes. The near-term priority is therefore not higher retrospective diagnostic performance alone, but reproducible, transparent, and prospectively evaluated integration into radiology workflows.

title: Prostate cancer screening with MRI: insights from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group.
abstract: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening for prostate cancer (PCa) remains controversial due to uncertain long-term benefits, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment of indolent disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has transformed the diagnostic pathway of PCa and is increasingly explored as a screening tool. This special report from the ESUR Prostate MRI Working Group provides an overview of current evidence and insights into the potential role of MRI in PCa screening. MRI-based screening strategies appear to improve detection of clinically significant PCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies and diagnoses of non-significant disease, though long-term outcome data, including mortality impact and interval cancer rates, remain limited. Biparametric MRI is particularly suited for screening due to its shorter acquisition time, reduced operational complexity, and lower costs compared with multiparametric MRI. Two main implementation approaches have emerged: MRI-first pathways, which maximise detection but require substantial resources, and risk-stratified strategies, in which MRI is used after initial assessment (e.g. PSA), potentially offering greater feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Evidence from large trials supports integrating MRI into screening pathways, particularly as a reflex test after PSA screening, although uncertainties remain regarding optimal protocols, interpretation thresholds, follow-up strategies, and long-term outcomes. Key barriers include limited MRI capacity, economic considerations, and the need for standardisation and quality assurance. Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance efficiency. Overall, MRI has the potential to improve the balance between benefits and harms in PCa screening, but further evidence is required to define its optimal implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can prostate MRI be effectively integrated into population-based prostate cancer screening pathways? Findings MRI-based screening improves detection of csPCa while reducing unnecessary biopsies; biparametric MRI should be the protocol of choice to enhance feasibility, although optimal implementation and long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Clinical relevance MRI may overcome key limitations of PSA-based screening by enhancing the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer while reducing harms such as overdiagnosis and unnecessary biopsies.

title: The role of cardiac CT with late iodine enhancement in patients with acute cardiac symptoms and troponin elevation in the era of high-sensitivity assays.
abstract: Objectives Diagnostic workup of patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no acute myocardial infarction (AMI) criteria is challenging. Cardiac CT angiography (CCTA) rules out obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Adding late iodine enhancement and extracellular volume fraction (CCTA + LIE/ECV) provides insights into myocardial injury. However, the impact on working diagnosis, agreement with discharge diagnosis, and mid-term safety of implementing CCTA + LIE/ECV in the emergency department remains uncertain. Materials and methods Prospective study on consecutive patients presenting, from June 2018 to February 2025, with acute chest pain or equivalents, elevated troponin, and no AMI diagnosis, excluding previously revascularized patients. Patients underwent CCTA to rule out obstructive CAD (≥ 50% stenosis). CCTA-negative patients underwent myocardial tissue characterization with LIE; if negative, ECV was quantified. Primary endpoint modification of working diagnosis by CT. Secondary endpoints: agreement between CT and discharge diagnoses after standard-of-care assessment; mid-term major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) in CT-negative patients. Results Among 191 patients (age 70 [55-79] years; 53% men), CCTA identified obstructive CAD in 76/191 (40%). LIE/ECV were positive in 58/106 (55%) of CCTA-negative cases, revealing myocarditis in 32/106 (30%), AMI with non-obstructive CAD in 8/106 (8%), Takotsubo in 14/106 (13%), amyloidosis in 3/106 (3%), and dilated cardiomyopathy in 1/106 (1%). CT modified the working diagnosis in 91/191 (48%) patients. Agreement between CT and discharge diagnosis was 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-0.97). In patients with negative CCTA + LIE/ECV, no MACEs occurred after 24 [interquartile range, 19-29] months. Conclusion In patients with acute symptoms, elevated troponin, and no AMI, a protocol combining CCTA + LIE/ECV enables etiologic assessment of coronary and myocardial conditions, refines working diagnosis, and entails a favorable prognosis when negative. Key points Question Patients with acute cardiac symptoms, troponin elevation, and no evidence of acute myocardial infarction represent a diagnostic challenge: cardiac CT with late iodine enhancement may have diagnostic and prognostic implications. Findings CT angiography with late iodine enhancement provided a diagnosis in 75% of patients and modified the working diagnosis in 48%. In the 25% CT-negative patients, no adverse events occurred at mid-term follow-up. Clinical relevance A CT protocol including coronary artery evaluation and myocardial tissue characterization may provide a rapid etiological diagnosis in patients with acute symptoms and troponin elevation, potentially supporting earlier clinical decision-making and reducing the need for additional downstream testing.

title: Low-dose vs standard-dose photon-counting CT for myopathy-associated interstitial lung disease: a prospective feasibility study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the clinical utility of photon counting computed tomography (PCCT)-derived quantitative parameters for assessing interstitial lung disease (ILD) burden in patients with inflammatory idiopathic myopathy (IIM), comparing standard-dose (SD) and tin-filtered low-dose (LD) protocols, and to assess the added value of ultrathin reconstructions. Materials and methods In this single-centre prospective study (September 2023-November 2024), outpatients with IIM-ILD underwent two consecutive PCCT scans. Quantitative ILD features were extracted using a commercial deep-learning software (ContextFlow ADVANCE Chest CT). Primary analyses compared LD 1.0 mm with SD 1.0 mm reconstructions using Bland-Altman analysis, with exploratory analyses of ultrathin (0.4 mm) reconstructions. Correlation analyses between deep learning-derived quantitative parameters, visual assessment, and pulmonary function tests were performed. Results Forty-eight adults with IIM-ILD (40 females; mean age, 53.88 ± 11.13 years) were included. The LD protocol achieved a substantial dose reduction (CTDIvol: 0.77 vs 5.40 mGy) while maintaining good agreement with SD (mean net differences [MNDs] < 1% for all patterns). LD-1.0 mm protocol yielded higher volume of ground-glass opacity (MND, 0.98%) and lower volume of fibrosis extent (MND, -0.64%). Reticular pattern showed strong association with FVC% (rho SD1.0mm = -0.62, p < 0.001) and DLCO% (rho SD1.0mm = -0.73, p < 0.001), with similar correlations observed under LD acquisition (Δrho ≤ 0.02). Ultrathin reconstructions yielded greater measurement of bronchiectasis (MND, 0.13% on SD scans). Conclusion LD PCCT serves as a radiation-sparing alternative for quantitative disease assessment. Ultrathin reconstructions provide limited additional value. Future longitudinal studies are warranted to validate the performance of LD PCCT for disease monitoring. Key points Question Can LD photon-counting CT provide robust quantitative assessment of ILD burden in patients with inflammatory myopathy compared with SD imaging? Findings Deep learning segmentation yielded LD ILD patterns that closely matched SD results, with all MNDs below 1%. Clinical relevance LD PCCT maintains quantitative robustness and physiological validity for IIM-ILD assessment, with total disease burden showing good agreement with the SD protocol, offering a radiation-sparing alternative without compromising CT-physiology correlation.

title: Retinal layer thickness as a potential marker for future cardiovascular events - a UK Biobank cohort study using optical coherence tomography.
abstract: Aims Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide. For CVD prevention, effective screening is needed to identify high-risk individuals. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides a noninvasive, low-cost "quick look" into the brain and has recently shown thinning of certain retinal layers in patients with previous CVD. We explored if OCT-derived retinal layer thicknesses could predict future major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: stroke/myocardial infarction/cardiovascular death). Methods In this retrospective cohort study, data of 51,293 participants from the UK Biobank were analyzed. We used cause-specific hazard models to evaluate the association of retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (RNFL) and ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) thickness with incident MACE, adjusting models for cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) and performed subanalyses for association with incident stroke and myocardial infarction. Results Median follow-up time was 14.7 years. Both RNFL thickness (aHR 0.92, 95% CI 0.89-0.96, p < 0.001) and GCIPL thickness (aHR 0.96, 95% CI 0.92-1.00, p = 0.04) were statistically associated with incident MACE in cause-specific hazard models adjusted for CVRF. Interestingly, RNFL thickness was more strongly associated with incident myocardial infarction (aHR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88-0.99, p = 0.02) while GCIPL was more strongly associated with incident stroke (aHR 0.90, 95% CI 0.83-0.96, p = 0.003). Conclusion RNFL and GCIPL thicknesses are associated with future MACE, even after adjusting for CVRF. OCT-measured retinal layer thickness could contribute to the assessment of cardiovascular risk.

title: MR spectroscopy in the diagnosis of lumbar discogenic pain.
abstract: Purpose to determine whether magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) provides similar clinical data to low pressure provocative discography (PD). Methods Twenty patients suffering from axial lower back pain underwent both MRS and PD concurrently. MRS was performed on a Siemens 3T scanner* of the lower three lumbar discs, where possible. Collapsed discs could not be assessed. Low pressure PD was performed on at least the lower three discs, by the author with considerable experience of the technique. Results MRS agreed with PD findings in 70-87% of 55 discs tested, depending on the agreement level set. Of the non-agreements, 10/17 were under-calls, 3 were overcalls and 4 were indeterminate. Conclusion MRS of lumbar discs may become a viable alternative to PD, as our experience and the technique evolves.

title: Automated 3D Analysis of Hip Morphology in a Young Adult Population.
abstract: Purpose Although many factors contribute to the development of hip OA, structural findings, such as acetabular dysplasia, are recognized as strong contributing factors to early degenerative changes. However, conventional two-dimensional imaging cannot fully capture the joint's three-dimensional anatomy. This study aimed to develop and validate an automated MRI-based method for 3D hip morphology analysis. Methods MRI data from 2,454 participants in the Generation R Cohort (1,199 males; 1,255 females; mean age 18.4 years; mean BMI 22.7 kg/m 2 ) were analyzed. An nnU-Net deep learning model, trained on 40 manually segmented hips, automatically segmented femoral bone, acetabular bone, and femoral and acetabular cartilage. Model performance was assessed using Dice scores. From the segmentations, five categories of morphological features were computed: basic geometric metrics, cartilage volumes, angular measurements, coverage metrics, and joint space width. Sex differences were evaluated using independent t-tests, and BMI-related differences using one-way ANOVA. Results The model achieved Dice scores of 0.97 for femoral bone, 0.90 for acetabular bone, 0.76 for femoral cartilage, and 0.77 for acetabular cartilage. Reference ranges were established for all biomarkers. Significant differences were observed between males and females and across BMI groups. Conclusion Automated 3D hip morphology analysis using MRI is feasible and reliable. The generated reference values enhance understanding of hip development and anatomical variation in young adults and support future large-scale, reproducible assessments. All developed code is made openly available at https://gitlab.com/radiology/msk/genr/hip/hip-segmentation-and-biomarkers.

title: Age-associated radiomic phenotyping in mice using multi-energy photon-counting and preclinical CT: an exploratory study.
abstract: To investigate whether CT-derived radiomic features capture imaging patterns associated with chronological age groups in mice and to assess the influence of imaging platform and photon-counting CT reconstruction strategy on classification performance. Female C57BL/6NRj mice from three chronological age groups (28, 88, and 99 weeks; n = 11) underwent clinical photon-counting CT (PCCT) and preclinical Albira II CT. Heart, liver, and spleen were segmented and radiomic features were extracted. The individual mouse was defined as the independent biological unit. Model development and evaluation used nested leave-one-mouse-out cross-validation with all preprocessing, feature selection, model selection, and, where applicable, reconstruction-energy selection restricted to the respective training folds. Organ-level class probabilities were averaged to generate one mouse-level prediction. Monoenergetic PCCT reconstructions from 40 to 180 keV were evaluated, including a fully nested energy-and-pipeline selection analysis. A grouped mouse-level permutation analysis with 200 permutations was performed for the primary monoenergetic workflow. Albira II correctly classified 5/11 mice (45.5%; 95% CI, 21.3-72.0%), whereas PCCT-SPP correctly classified 10/11 mice (90.9%; 95% CI, 62.3-98.4%). The fully nested monoenergetic PCCT workflow correctly classified 9/11 mice (81.8%; 95% CI, 52.3-94.9%; balanced accuracy, 83.3%; macro-F1, 83.3%). Energy-specific performance varied considerably: 110 keV showed the highest accuracy (81.8%) and was selected in 7/11 outer folds, whereas the highest macro one-vs-rest AUC occurred at 130 keV (0.867). None of the 200 permuted analyses reached the observed fully nested monoenergetic accuracy (plus-one corrected Monte-Carlo p = 0.005). CT-derived radiomic features showed chronological age-group-associated patterns in this exploratory murine cohort, with classification performance varying substantially across imaging platforms and reconstruction strategies. PCCT-SPP showed the numerically highest performance, while monoenergetic PCCT demonstrated pronounced energy dependence without evidence for a universally optimal reconstruction energy. These findings require validation in larger independent cohorts and correlation with independent biological-aging reference measures.

title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Value of Sonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter in Patients with Ischemic Stroke or Hypertensive Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Background Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a critical complication in nontraumatic brain injury, yet invasive monitoring carries significant risks, and noninvasive alternatives remain undervalidated. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) ultrasonography represents a promising bedside technique, but data in nontraumatic populations are limited. This study evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of ONSD in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. Methods This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 100 neurocritical intensive care unit (ICU) patients with acute nontraumatic brain injury [ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage; Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) < 9] who underwent admission computed tomography (CT) and bedside ONSD ultrasonography. Sixty age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers were enrolled exclusively to provide descriptive reference values for physiological ONSD and were not included in the primary diagnostic or prognostic analyses. CT-based radiologic ICP surrogates were the reference standard. Exploratory analyses evaluated inter-eye variability, adjusted models, and in-hospital survival. Results ONSD increased stepwise across healthy controls, patients with negative CT, and patients with positive CT (4.62 ± 0.33, 5.52 ± 0.51, and 6.50 ± 0.51 mm, respectively). Among neurocritical patients, a cohort-derived cutoff of ≥ 6.00 mm yielded 86.7% sensitivity, 85.0% specificity, 89.7% positive predictive value, 81.0% negative predictive value, 86.0% accuracy, and 0.901 area under the curve (AUC). Above-threshold ONSD remained independently associated with CT-positive elevated ICP after adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), GCS, and systolic blood pressure (SBP) in exploratory multivariable analysis. Exploratory survival analysis showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality in patients with ONSD above the cohort-derived threshold (log-rank p = 4.77 × 10 -13 ). Conclusions Bedside ultrasonographic ONSD measurement appears clinically useful for early triage and longitudinal bedside surveillance in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly when invasive monitoring is unavailable or delayed.

CT-based radiologic ICP surrogates were the reference standard. Exploratory analyses evaluated inter-eye variability, adjusted models, and in-hospital survival.

Results

ONSD increased stepwise across healthy controls, patients with negative CT, and patients with positive CT (4.62 ± 0.33, 5.52 ± 0.51, and 6.50 ± 0.51 mm, respectively). Among neurocritical patients, a cohort-derived cutoff of ≥ 6.00 mm yielded 86.7% sensitivity, 85.0% specificity, 89.7% positive predictive value, 81.0% negative predictive value, 86.0% accuracy, and 0.901 area under the curve (AUC). Above-threshold ONSD remained independently associated with CT-positive elevated ICP after adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), GCS, and systolic blood pressure (SBP) in exploratory multivariable analysis. Exploratory survival analysis showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality in patients with ONSD above the cohort-derived threshold (log-rank p = 4.77 × 10-13).

Conclusions

Bedside ultrasonographic ONSD measurement appears clinically useful for early triage and longitudinal bedside surveillance in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly when invasive monitoring is unavailable or delayed.

title: Resistance Phenotypes and Treatment Sequencing After Immune Checkpoint Blockade in MSI-H/dMMR Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Review.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed microsatellite instability-high or mismatch repair-deficient metastatic colorectal cancer, but clinically relevant progression still occurs and treatment after progression remains undefined. We performed a clinically oriented narrative review, updated August 8, 2026, and separated direct prospective evidence, retrospective post-ICI evidence, extrapolation from general metastatic colorectal cancer trials, case-level evidence, and biological rationale. In the absence of prospective post-dual-ICI sequencing studies, we propose an evidence-informed conceptual framework. Apparent early progression should prompt confirmation of MSI/MMR status and exclusion of pseudoprogression before classification as early global progression, late systemic progression, or oligoprogression. BRAF V600E is common in MSI-H/dMMR metastatic colorectal cancer and is not an absolute predictor of ICI failure, but it is a major treatment-defining branch after progression. Repeat tissue biopsy or circulating tumor DNA profiling should be selective, used when findings can alter management and without delaying urgent therapy. ctDNA-based molecular residual disease is prognostic after curative-intent colorectal cancer resection, including metastasectomy, but is not validated to direct treatment of radiographically evident post-ICI progression. Oligoprogression warrants multidisciplinary consideration of local therapy, while ICI rechallenge remains investigational. Most recommendations are retrospective or extrapolated; transparent evidence boundaries and prospective post-dual-ICI studies are essential.

title: Mammography and Ultrasonography for Symptomatic Male Breast Lesions: A PRISMA-DTA Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Male breast disease is uncommon, but symptomatic men require reliable differentiation between benign conditions and lesions warranting biopsy or oncologic management. This PRISMA-DTA (Preferred Reporting Items for a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies) systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic accuracy, clinical utility, and evidentiary limitations of mammography and ultrasonography for malignant versus benign male breast lesions. Materials and methods PubMed, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 30, 2026. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO before journal submission (CRD420261429183). Eligible reports evaluated mammography or ultrasonography in male breast disease and provided extractable 2 × 2 diagnostic data. Methodological quality was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized separately for each modality using bivariate random-effects modeling and summary receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results Thirteen eligible reports were included. Seven mammography datasets and five ultrasonography datasets were available for quantitative synthesis. Mammography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.840 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.705-0.921) and a specificity of 0.951 (95% CI, 0.884-0.980), whereas ultrasonography showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.775-0.941) and a specificity of 0.958 (95% CI, 0.869-0.987). Although pooled specificity estimates were high, their magnitude may have been influenced by heterogeneous diagnostic thresholds, differential verification, variable follow-up, and sparse malignant case counts. Nine of 13 reports were judged to have an overall high risk of bias, and consistent paired head-to-head data were lacking. Conclusion Current evidence supports mammography and ultrasonography as complementary tools in risk-stratified assessment of symptomatic male breast lesions. Pooled estimates should be interpreted cautiously because the evidence base is small and methodologically limited. Current data do not establish direct modality superiority, do not justify biopsy avoidance when clinical-imaging discordance persists, and do not determine the incremental value of routine combined imaging.

title: <sup>18</sup>F-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET in Rheumatologic and Autoimmune Disorders.
abstract: FDG PET detects the silent inflammation of autoimmune and rheumatologic diseases even before tissue damage, as activated leukocytes overexpress glucose transporters. It has an important role in large vessel vasculitis which includes early diagnosis, disease monitoring and response assessment to treatment. In inflammatory arthritides, it quantifies synovitis and enthesitis and detects early treatment response. In connective tissue and immunoglobulin G4 related diseases, whole body imaging maps silent disease, helps exclude malignancy, and guides biopsy. It is central to cardiac sarcoidosis and an early test in fever of unknown origin.

title: Interpretable CT-based radiomics nomogram integrating clinical and semantic features for preoperative grading of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms: a shap-based analysis.
abstract: Preoperative grading of pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (PNENs) is crucial for personalized management. This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning framework based on CT imaging to predict PNENs pathological grades. We retrospectively analyzed 125 patients with pathologically confirmed PNENs, divided into training and test cohorts. A comprehensive radiomics pipeline was implemented, involving the extraction of high-dimensional features from CT images. We constructed three predictive models: a clinical model, a radiomics model, and a fusion model. To ensure methodological robustness, seven machine-learning algorithms were employed and cross-validated to identify the optimal classifier. Furthermore, the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method was utilized to decode the "black box" of the radiomics signature. The fusion model-integrating CT radiomic signatures with semantic hallmarks-consistently outperformed the standalone clinical and radiomics models, achieving a superior AUC of 0.891 in the validation cohort. SHAP analysis revealed that microscopic texture complexity (e.g., Zone Entropy) and macro-geometric irregularity (e.g., Sphericity) were the dominant predictors, aligning with the biological aggressiveness of high-grade lesions. By integrating multi-dimensional CT features with a rigorous machine-learning consensus, our study provides a highly accurate and interpretable "virtual biopsy" tool.

title: Core Descriptor Set for Studies Evaluating Interventions for Chronic Deep Venous Diseases.
abstract: Objective Chronic deep venous disease (CDVD) is a common and debilitating disease resulting in significant morbidity and costs. However, inconsistent reporting of patient characteristics in CDVD hinders study comparability and limits opportunities for data synthesis. This study aimed to develop a core descriptor set (CDS) for studies evaluating interventions for CDVD of the lower limbs. Methods Candidate descriptors were identified from published literature and stakeholder recommendations. Vascular surgeons, haematologists, interventional radiologists, and nurse specialists took part in two rounds of an international modified Delphi process using a nine point Likert scale to rank descriptor importance. Descriptors not meeting consensus criteria in the first round were re-evaluated in round two. Descriptors meeting the criteria for critical importance were discussed in a final meeting between international specialists to finalise the CDS. Results One hundred and thirty-eight Delphi participants were recruited from 29 countries. Ninety-eight descriptors were longlisted from the literature, refined to 84 by the steering group. After round one, 23 descriptors achieved consensus and were removed from subsequent rounds. Seven newly proposed descriptors were then added, resulting in a total of 68 descriptors in round two. Following round two, a further 13 descriptors achieved consensus with eight considered borderline. Following two Delphi survey rounds and a consensus meeting, 84 candidate descriptors were systematically evaluated and narrowed down to a final set of 21 core descriptors across the domains of demographics, thrombotic risk, venous history, anatomy, symptoms, and clinical findings. Conclusion This study defined the CDS for CDVD, facilitating more consistent, robust, and meaningful reporting across studies and enabling reliable synthesis.

title: Using Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance to Improve Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease Risk Stratification in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes from Primary Care and Endocrinology Settings.
abstract: Objectives Current metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) guidelines recommend fibrosis screening in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) because of their increased risk of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2). However, fibrosis risk is variable, and clinical tools to identify individuals at lower risk are lacking. We evaluated whether assessment of insulin resistance by homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) could improve risk stratification for clinically significant fibrosis. Methods We prospectively recruited 501 adults with T2D from primary care and endocrinology clinics. Participants were classified as insulin-resistant (HOMA-IR ≥2.5; n=350) or insulin-sensitive (HOMA-IR <2.5; n=151). Liver steatosis was assessed using VCTE, MRI/MRE, or liver biopsy according to the most accurate test, and the prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was compared between groups. Results Insulin-resistant participants had higher prevalence of clinically significant fibrosis than insulin-sensitive participants (≥F2: 10% vs. <1%; p<0.001). They also had greater hepatic steatosis, higher ALT, AST, CK-18, HbA1c, and adipose tissue insulin resistance (Adipo-IR) levels, and lower adiponectin concentrations (all p<0.001). Fibrosis was infrequent among insulin-sensitive participants and almost exclusively limited to mild fibrosis (stage F1). Among participants with steatosis, ≥F2 fibrosis was present in 1% of insulin-sensitive participants compared with 13% of insulin-resistant participants (p<0.001). Conclusions Clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2) was uncommon among insulin-sensitive individuals with T2D and largely limited to mild fibrosis (F1). HOMA-IR <2.5 identified a subgroup at very low risk for fibrosis, supporting its potential use as a simple, clinically accessible tool for MASLD risk stratification in primary care and endocrinology settings.

title: Machine Learning Models Combining [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET Radiomics and Clinical Features to Predict Overall Survival for Metastatic Castration-resistant Prostate Cancer Treated with [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligand Therapy.
abstract: Purpose Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains incurable despite recent therapeutic advances. [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (lutetium-177 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy) provides meaningful clinical benefit in selected patients. However, ∼30% of the patients do not respond to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Although several baseline prognostic factors are well known, reliable pretherapeutic predictive biomarkers are still lacking. We developed and compared several predictive machine learning (ML) models integrating clinical, biochemical, and imaging data, including [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET (gallium-68 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen ligand positron emission tomography) radiomic features, to estimate overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Methods This retrospective monocentric study included 102 patients with mCRPC treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA between January 2022 and March 2024. title: Clinical T staging accuracy and its prognostic relevance in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Accurate clinical T-staging is essential for guiding surgical management in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), particularly when determining treatment escalation or de-escalation. This study evaluated its diagnostic accuracy and impact on potential over- and undertreatment. This retrospective single-center study included patients with histologically confirmed OSCC who underwent primary surgical resection with negative margins between 2012 and 2022. Clinical T-staging based on preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical examination was compared with pathological staging. The primary endpoint was the diagnostic accuracy of clinical T-staging, while secondary endpoints were overall survival and disease-free survival. A total of 637 patients were included in this study, from which 33.9% were inaccurately staged. Clinical stages T1 and T4a yielded the highest accuracy (81.6% and 84.1%), while stages T2 and T3 only had 69.2% and 64.3%. Midline tumors and patients with a clinically unsuspicious neck (cN0) were more frequently staged accurately. In survival analysis, inaccurate T-staging was not independently associated with worse overall survival (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% confidence interval 0.65-1.27, P = 0.59) or disease-free survival (1.02, 0.70-1.49, P = 0.93). Clinical T staging in OSCC was inaccurate in approximately one-third of cases, particularly in cT2-3 tumors, whereas cT1 and cT4a showed higher concordance. Although staging inaccuracies were not linked to survival, they may influence the extent of surgical resection and the overall invasiveness of the procedure.

title: Optimizing Echocardiographic Evaluation of Chronic Mitral Regurgitation: Comparison With Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Implications for Guideline Recommendations.
abstract: Background The ASE (American Society of Echocardiography) guidelines recommend the presence of at least 4 specific criteria to confirm a diagnosis of definite severe mitral regurgitation (MR). However, the performance of these criteria, particularly when <4 are present, remains unclear. Objectives This study aims to evaluate and optimize the ASE native MR guidelines by comparing them with quantitative cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), considered the reference standard for MR assessment. Methods In this prospective study, 177 patients underwent near-simultaneous CMR and transthoracic echocardiography for the assessment of MR. MR severity was classified using a 4-grade scale based on CMR-derived regurgitant volume, which was calculated as the difference between total left ventricular (LV) stroke volume and aortic forward flow. MR severity was similarly graded using the ASE algorithm, with quantification performed when necessary, by averaging the regurgitant volume from 3 methods: 1) the proximal isovelocity surface area method; 2) the biplane LV volumetric method; and 3) the mitral valve volumetric method. Results The study cohort had a median age of 61.7 years, with 55% being men. Primary MR was the predominant pathology (73% of patients), with 42% having mitral valve prolapse and 25% presenting with flail leaflets. There was exact agreement between transthoracic echocardiography and CMR MR grading in 51% of cases, whereas agreement within 1 grade was observed in 89%. Patients who met any of the ASE severe MR criteria were predominantly classified as having grades 3 to 4 MR by CMR. The following ASE parameters demonstrated high specificity for identifying grade 4 MR by CMR: pulmonary vein systolic flow reversal (specificity 88%), enlarged LV with normal systolic function (specificity 85%), proximal isovelocity surface area radius ≥1.0 cm (specificity 83%), and vena contracta width ≥0.7 cm (specificity 80%). Combining color Doppler with either pulmonary vein systolic reversal or enlarged LV with normal function resulted in 91%-95% specificity for severe MR. Importantly, reliance on fewer ASE criteria reduced the need for quantification from 86% (4 criteria) to 73% (3 criteria) and 59% (2 criteria), thereby enhancing diagnostic efficiency. Conclusions Certain ASE criteria, especially when used in combination, are highly specific for diagnosing severe MR, even when <4 criteria are present. This study suggests that in many cases, the reliance on extensive quantification may be reduced, streamlining the diagnostic process and improving clinical workflow.

title: Differentiation of common liver tumors using tumor-to-liver contrast on routine non-contrast T 2 -weighted magnetic resonance imaging.
abstract: Introduction Accurate classification of liver tumors requires contrast-enhanced MRI. However, contrast agents are contraindicated in patients with renal impairment or allergies. Concerns regarding the environmental impact of gadolinium-based agents have increased. Thus, classification using non-contrast MRI is desirable. This study evaluated whether tumor-to-liver contrast (TLC) derived from T 2 -weighted imaging (T 2 WI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), along with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), can differentiate common liver tumors: hepatocellular carcinomas (HCCs), metastases, and hemangiomas. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 119 patients with 122 liver tumors undergoing liver MRI. We calculated TLC from T 2 WI and DWI (b = 1000 s/mm²), and measured ADC values. Tumors were classified as HCCs, metastases, or hemangiomas based on radiological or pathological findings. Analyses were stratified by liver function using the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score. Group differences were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis and Steel-Dwass tests. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using one-versus-rest receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results T 2 WI-derived TLC differed significantly among tumor types (p < 0.05) and was highest in hemangiomas, followed by metastases and HCCs. DWI-derived TLC and ADC values differed in some tumor comparisons but showed greater variability and overlap. These patterns persisted after ALBI stratification. ROC analysis showed that T 2 WI-derived TLC performed well for hemangiomas (AUC = 0.975) and HCC (AUC = 0.839), whereas ADC performed best for metastases (AUC = 0.716). Overall, T 2 WI-derived TLC outperformed DWI-derived TLC. Conclusions TLC derived from non-contrast T 2 WI may serve as a practical, observer-independent marker for differentiating liver tumors, particularly in patients who cannot receive contrast agents. Plain language summary MRI scans with contrast agents are often used to identify different types of liver tumors, but some people cannot safely receive these agents. This study reviewed MRI scans from people with liver tumors and examined whether measurements from standard non-contrast MRI images could help distinguish between common tumor types. This study found that a measurement taken from T 2 -weighted MRI images was particularly effective at differentiating liver tumors, especially hemangiomas and hepatocellular carcinoma, without the need for contrast agents. This matters because non-contrast MRI methods may help support diagnosis in people who cannot receive contrast agents and may reduce reliance on these substances.

title: Accelerated 3D Late Gadolinium Enhancement Pulse Sequence with Isotropic Spatial Resolution, Self-Navigation of Respiratory Motion, and Arrhythmia Rejection for Quantification of Left Atrial Fibrosis in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation.
abstract: Background The left atrium (LA) is a thin structure (1.5-2.5mm). Conventional 3D late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) pulse sequences for imaging the LA typically have limited through-plane resolution (2.5-5mm) or prolonged scan times (10-15min), resulting in poor image quality and limited clinical translatability. We sought to develop and test whether a 3D LGE pulse sequence featuring 1.5mm³ isotropic spatial resolution and a predictable scan time of 600 heartbeats can produce diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T for quantification of LA structural remodeling in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Methods A 3D LGE pulse sequence was developed using gradient-recalled echo (GRE) readout, stack-of-stars k-space sampling with variable density along the partition direction, retrospective arrhythmia rejection, and XD-GRASP reconstruction with self-navigation of respiratory motion. Thirty patients with AF (twenty imaged prior to first-time ablation, ten prior to repeat ablation) and twenty healthy controls were scanned using this pulse sequence. The upper limit of normal image intensity ratio (IIR) was derived from the control group; specifically, 2 standard deviations (SDs) above the mean. Suspected LA fibrosis was quantified by one rater. Two cardiothoracic radiologists independently graded the image quality across three categories (conspicuity, artifacts, noise) using a 5-point Likert scale per category, with a score of 3 considered clinically acceptable. Results The proposed pulse sequence produced diagnostically acceptable image quality scores in all three categories for AF and control cohorts. Retrospective rejection of data acquired during ectopic heartbeats significantly (p<0.05) improved contrast-to-noise ratio (+3.7%) and sharpness (blur metric -3.2%) metrics, albeit at the expense of a significantly reduced signal-to-noise ratio (-4.4%). The upper limit of normal IIR was 1.43. Using this cutoff value to identify suspected LA fibrosis, compared with the control group (2.47 ± 2.24%), the first-time ablation group (7.45 ± 7.38%) was not significantly different (p = 0.14), whereas the repeat ablation group (14.94 ± 13.83%) was significantly different (p < 0.05). Conclusion The proposed pulse sequence produces diagnostically acceptable image quality at 1.5T and provides evidence of LA structural remodeling in AF patients, including greater suspected LA fibrosis burden, relative to control subjects.

title: VIRTUAL REALITY-ENHANCED FOR PREOPERATIVE ANATOMICAL ASSESSMENT OF ABDOMINAL NEUROBLASTOMA: A COMPARATIVE STUDY WITH CONVENTIONAL CT IMAGING.
abstract: Aim Accurate assessment of tumour anatomy is critical for neuroblastoma surgical planning. This study evaluated whether patient-specific virtual reality (VR) models improve the accuracy of pre-operative anatomical assessment compared with conventional computed tomography (CT) imaging. Methods CT scans from nine patients with abdominal neuroblastoma were segmented to create patient-specific VR models, which were then imported into an in-house VR application. Eleven paediatric surgeons (n=5 consultants; n=6 registrars) independently evaluated conventional CT images and VR reconstructions to assess vascular and organ involvement, image-defined risk factors (IDRFs), and operative strategies. Anatomical accuracy was quantified against intraoperative findings recorded in the International Neuroblastoma Surgical Report Form. Subjective ratings were collected using Likert scales. Mixed-effects models and non-parametric statistical analyses were conducted (p<0.05). Results VR significantly improved overall anatomical accuracy, with a mean increase of 12.4 percentage points (95% CI 8.5-16.3; p<0.0001). Improvements were observed for vascular involvement (+12.5%, p<0.001), organ involvement (+9.6%, p<0.01), and IDRF identification (+13.7%, p<0.0001). Improvements in anatomical accuracy with VR were similar between consultants and registrars. VR did not significantly alter operative planning decisions or predicted tumour resectability. Surgeons reported greater confidence in anatomical understanding and surgical planning with VR than CT (p<0.001). The VR platform received high ratings for usability, integration into the preoperative planning workflow, and perceived clinical value. Conclusion VR improved surgeons' anatomical assessment accuracy and confidence compared with traditional CT scans, highlighting VR's potential as a useful supplement to conventional imaging for preoperative evaluation in complex abdominal neuroblastoma.

title: Utilizing light energy transformation in nanostructures for targeted diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Theranostics, a combination of therapy and diagnostics, represents a paradigm change in precision medicine with the ability to monitor diseases in real time and deliver targeted treatment. Nanomaterials are state-of-the-art technology for photo-energy conversion-based therapeutic action and diagnostic imaging; note the remarkable temporal and spatial precision that uses light as a driving force. This review highlights recent advances in the design and application of such nanomaterials for converting light into demand responses via mechanisms including photoluminescence (PL), photothermal conversion for photothermal therapy (PTT), photoacoustic imaging (PAI), photoelectric effect, SERS-based detection, and photodynamic therapy (PDT). Such light-activated systems are versatile platforms for the treatment of various diseases like arthritis, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and retinal degeneration. By integrating multiple therapeutic and diagnostic modalities into a single nanoscale system, photoactive nanomaterials hold the potential to achieve enhanced treatment efficacy with minimal side effects. However, rapid advances are still hindered by challenges related to maximizing tissue penetration and biocompatibility, as well as activation in physiological settings. Nevertheless, the synergy of light-based science and nanotechnology is enabling next-generation precision theranostics and dynamic tools for personalized medicine for physicians. For these intelligent nanoplatforms to reach their full potential in practical healthcare applications, more interdisciplinary research and clinical translation are required.
