title: Photoacoustic imaging of human brain function through intact adult skulls
abstract: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized noninvasive imaging of human brain function, but it indirectly senses deoxyhemoglobin through water-proton relaxation and relies on bulky, costly, noisy, enclosed, superconducting-magnet scanners. In contrast, photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) directly probes hemoglobin absorption using a more compact, lower-cost, quieter, open, magnet-free system. However, functional PACT of the adult human brain has so far been demonstrated only after surgical skull removal, because the skull strongly attenuates optical and acoustic signals. Here, we demonstrate non-invasive transcranial functional PACT (T-fPACT) through the intact adult skull. A densely packed, high-channel-count (3,072-element) hemispherical ultrasonic array provides near-$2π$-steradian simultaneous acquisition, enabling high sensitivity and single-shot three-dimensional imaging at 20 Hz that eliminates motion blurring. Participant-specific stabilization further enables measurement of small task-evoked hemodynamic responses over the entire task duration. In healthy adults, T-fPACT localized responses to expected sensorimotor regions, distinguished task-specific motor representations, and yielded consistent localizations across repeated task runs and visits. Comparison with high-field (7 T) fMRI showed spatially corresponding functional regions, while dual-wavelength imaging revealed distinct hemoglobin-weighted responses. These findings overcome the long-standing skull barrier in human brain PACT and establish non-invasive, rapid volumetric photoacoustic imaging of brain function.

title: SPARCL: Spatially Adaptive Regional Coverage for Active Learning in Chest X-ray Analysis
abstract: Pixel-level annotation for chest X-ray (CXR) lesion segmentation is expensive, making active learning (AL) essential. However, existing AL strategies fail to account for the spatial distribution of selected samples, resulting in inconsistent performance across focal (e.g., aortic calcification) and diffuse (e.g., nodules) pathologies. In this paper, we propose SPARCL (Spatially Adaptive Regional Coverage for Active Learning) to dynamically balance predictive uncertainty with cumulative spatial coverage. By employing a concave coverage function, SPARCL imposes diminishing returns on previously annotated regions, naturally directing the annotation budget toward under-labeled areas. Furthermore, an entropy gate reverts the algorithm to standard uncertainty sampling when spatial variation is absent. This coverage objective is monotone submodular, guaranteeing near-optimal greedy batch selection. To address how aggregate metrics like Dice obscure regional failures, we further introduce two metrics---Spatial Inconsistency (SI) and Performance Coverage (PC)---to quantify anatomical fairness across AL rounds. Evaluated on an in-house calcification cohort and public CXR benchmarks, SPARCL reaches 95% of fully supervised performance using only 24% of the data, compared to 29% for the best baseline. Ultimately, SPARCL ensures robust spatial reliability, surfacing regional gains that aggregate metrics miss.

title: HierarchiRetina: A Diabetic Retinopathy Screening and Grading Cascade with Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Clinical screening for diabetic retinopathy proceeds in stages, yet most automated systems grade fundus images with a single black-box network. Three gaps remain: (i) lesions differ widely in size and contrast, but segmenters typically apply the same blocks to all; (ii) ungradable images are usually excluded or treated as an extra class, and lesion-aware graders seldom test whether lesions drive the grade; (iii) staged systems often report each stage only on the images reaching it, leaving propagated errors unmeasured. HierarchiRetina, a screening, segmentation and grading cascade with inspectable stage outputs, addresses each gap. First, HSMoE-AUNet is a U-Net whose skip, bottleneck and decoder blocks are sparse mixtures of heterogeneous experts, with lesion-matched types, counts and losses; SwinHRUNetPP, a dual-encoder vessel segmenter, uses a field-of-view-restricted loss. Second, LG-DRG separates gradability from ordinal severity and lets lesion masks query the image through gated cross-attention. Third, an end-to-end evaluation counts screening misses as errors and traces each error to its stage. Pooled Dice ranged from 0.184 (microaneurysms) to 0.579 (exudates); vessel Dice was 0.731. On 58,689 held-out images from six datasets, end-to-end quadratic weighted kappa was 0.804, with referral sensitivity 0.832 at specificity 0.947, and the screening gate caused 66% of errors. In ablations, the grade ignored the masks, even with the cross-attention gate started open. On all 4,105 official DDR test images, six-class accuracy was 85.6%, above the best published six-class result we found (83.8%). Staged screening systems should be evaluated end-to-end, with stage attribution and mask ablation, before clinical deployment.

title: AI-Enhanced Hyperspectral Imaging for Intraoperative Detection of Low-Grade Glioma: A Clinical Study
abstract: Current image-guided neuronavigation techniques, such as intraoperative MRI and ultrasound, are limited by high costs, limited sensitivity and operational complexity. There is a clear need for more efficient systems to enhance intra-operative tumor detection and improve patient outcomes for intrinsic brain tumor resection. Whereas previous intraoperative brain HSI studies have predominantly investigated high-grade gliomas, glioblastomas, or mixed-grade cohorts, this clinical study focuses specifically on low-grade gliomas (LGGs). LGGs strongly resemble normal brain under white light conditions on the operative microscope. This study characterizes spectral differences between healthy and tumor tissue and provides a paired comparison of HSI- and RGB-based classification at matched tissue locations and under identical patient-level data splits. Tumor regions showed consistently lower reflectance, which may be associated with differences in hemoglobin concentration and oxygenation. A range of classification models was evaluated. The 3D CNN, which integrates spectral and spatial features, achieved the highest median ROC-AUC of 74.5%, compared with 67.9% for the spectral-only XGBoost model and 64.0% for the RGB-based model. These results support further investigation of HSI for low-grade glioma classification and quantify its performance relative to conventional RGB imaging in this cohort.

title: FETALFusion: Resolution-Aware State-Space Modeling for Multi-Domain Fetal Head Segmentation
abstract: Head circumference (HC) measured from 2D ultrasound is a routine marker of fetal growth, and automating it needs segmentations whose boundaries hold up on individual scans, not only on average. We present FETALFusion, a dual-path CNN-Mamba encoder-decoder for fetal head segmentation across acquisition types. It applies four-directional state-space scans only at the two highest-resolution stages, routes bottleneck features through domain-specific channel gates that are averaged at test time, and adds a weak landmark shape prior. We train jointly on transabdominal (HC-18) and transperineal (PSFHS) images and compare ten methods on a held-out test set of 471 images, each trained under one schedule and scored by surface distances at native resolution. FETALFusion reaches a Dice score of 0.963 and an HD95 of 2.10 mm without test-time augmentation or a domain label. It improves on U-Mamba on all five reported metrics (HD95 reduced by 0.31 mm; Holm-corrected ($p < 10^{-4}$), a lead that holds under test-time augmentation and across two independent training runs, and in the mean on U-Net, Attention U-Net and TransUNet. Residual encoders close the gap: a ResNet-34 UNet++ exceeds FETALFusion, and an ImageNet initialised ResNet-34 U-Net is best overall (HD95 1.75 mm). The ablation agrees. Calibrated against run-to-run variation, it attributes FETALFusion's measurable gains to the landmark shape prior and, on transperineal images, to the domain gates, while removing the state-space branch does not measurably change accuracy. HC from the predicted masks agrees with the clinical reference at an intraclass correlation of 0.9986.

Residual encoders close the gap: a ResNet-34 UNet++ exceeds FETALFusion, and an ImageNet initialised ResNet-34 U-Net is best overall (HD95 1.75 mm). The ablation agrees. Calibrated against run-to-run variation, it attributes FETALFusion's measurable gains to the landmark shape prior and, on transperineal images, to the domain gates, while removing the state-space branch does not measurably change accuracy. HC from the predicted masks agrees with the clinical reference at an intraclass correlation of 0.9986.

title: dMRI-F: A Foundation Model for Generalizable Diffusion MRI Analysis from Sparse Acquisitions
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) probes water diffusion within the brain, providing unique information about tissue microstructure and white matter connectivity. High-quality dMRI enables advanced and accurate analyses but demands dense acquisitions, resulting in long scan times and hardware constraints that are often infeasible. Further, dMRI requires dedicated computational methods to support diverse analysis tasks (e.g., parcellation, registration, and synthesis) for both neuroscientific and clinical applications. Here, we present dMRI-F, a foundation model that unifies dMRI data enhancement and downstream tasks across diverse acquisitions and populations, while requiring only minimal acquisition input. dMRI-F is pre-trained with a q-space masked reconstruction task: predicting densely sampled multi-shell data from only six volumes. It learns generalizable latent feature representations of dMRI data, which serve as a core foundation for adapting to diverse downstream tasks, including brain parcellation, brain registration, and cross-modal synthesis. Across nine independently acquired datasets, we demonstrate that dMRI-F outperforms state-of-the-art methods with robust generalization across acquisitions, populations, and tasks. Our results demonstrate dMRI-F's versatility as a general-purpose framework that enables diverse dMRI applications from low-cost, sparse acquisitions.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

title: Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration for Dual-Student Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Dual-student learning enriches predictive diversity in SSMIS by introducing a strongly augmented view alongside a weakly augmented view. Insufficient strong augmentation may homogenize the students, whereas excessive augmentation can corrupt anatomical evidence and destabilize collaboration. This challenge echoes feedback-regulated human instruction, where learners receive differentiated tasks and the task difficulty is continually adjusted according to their evolving responses. Inspired by these, we propose Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration (HAC), a closed-loop dual-student framework that maintains weak--strong learning through adaptive difficulty calibration and geometry preservation. Specifically, Reinforcement-guided Difficulty Calibration (RDC) formulates strong-augmentation control as a window-level reinforcement learning process, using augmentation history, realized perturbations, and training responses to dynamically adjust the augmentation magnitude, operation number, and magnitude range. Meanwhile, the Gramian Geometry Preservation Constraint (G2PC) preserves the early-stage three-branch geometry through global volume and pairwise area constraints, preventing shared supervision from homogenizing the two students. Comprehensive evaluations across LA, Pancreas, and BraTS-2019 validate both the segmentation effectiveness and capability-aware difficulty calibration of HAC.

title: LiFUSE: Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining for Liver Disease Analysis on Non-contrast CT
abstract: Given the growing global burden of liver tumors and diffuse liver diseases, non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is increasingly used for opportunistic screening because of its low cost and favorable safety profile. However, downstream tasks such as tumor detection and fine-grained disease diagnosis remain challenging due to NCCT's inherently low tissue contrast, lack of hemodynamic enhancement, and complex anatomical background. These limitations make subtle, heterogeneous, and multifocal hepatic lesions difficult to identify. Although large-scale self-supervised pretraining can learn robust representations from unlabeled NCCT scans, conventional voxel-wise reconstruction does not fully exploit the complementary information available in NCCT. Under weak NCCT contrast, low-level intensity patterns become less informative for pathology recognition, limiting the capture of lesion-specific discriminative features. In this paper, we propose the Liver Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining (LiFUSE). The frequency branch applies random band-stop masking and spectrum reconstruction to encourage the model to capture subtle differences between lesions and surrounding tissues, while the spatial branch performs hybrid-granularity masked volumetric reconstruction to accommodate lesions of diverse sizes and morphologies. Finally, a cross-domain consistency scheme couples the spatial and frequency branches, yielding more discriminative representations for hepatic structures and lesions. Extensive experiments on three clinically relevant tasks across internal cohorts and a public target-domain transfer setting show that LiFUSE consistently outperforms strong baselines. These results suggest that unified frequency-spatial learning can improve liver disease analysis on NCCT, highlighting its potential for large-scale screening.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP: Plug-and-Play Denoising for Scientific Imaging with Self-Supervised Score Priors
abstract: Modern image restoration methods increasingly rely on large-scale supervised training, yet clean targets are often prohibitively difficult to obtain in scientific imaging modalities such as hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Plug-and-play ADMM (PnP-ADMM) with pretrained diffusion priors offers a promising alternative, but the learned prior distribution can mismatch both the target scientific image distribution and the distribution of ADMM denoiser inputs induced by dual feedback. To mitigate these mismatches, we propose $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP, a self-supervised plug-and-play restoration framework that learns a score prior directly from observation-derived ADMM intermediate states, without clean training targets or externally pretrained weights. Specifically, the learned score corrects the input to the analytical prior update, combining observation-driven corrections with analytical regularization. We further analyze the convergence and reconstruction error of the corrected ADMM algorithm assuming an ideal score and quadratic data fidelity. Experiments on reference-guided HSI restoration, single-image HSI denoising, and MRI denoising demonstrate consistent improvements over competing methods.

title: Dual-Domain Sparse-View 4D CBCT Reconstruction with Spatial-Temporal Consistency Learning
abstract: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D CBCT) provides phase-resolved volumetric images for image-guided radiotherapy. Yet good reconstruction quality usually needs many projections. This increases scan time and radiation dose. We propose STCNet, a sparse-view 4D CBCT reconstruction framework that uses spatial-temporal consistency learning. STCNet reconstructs high-quality images from only 16 projections in each respiratory phase. STCNet integrates physics-driven positional encoding to enforce geometric consistency in the projection domain and introduces temporal encoding in latent space to capture respiratory motion dynamics across phases to capture dynamic respiratory motion across phases. A dual-domain collaborative strategy jointly optimizes both projection and image domains, enhancing structural fidelity and temporal coherence. We tested STCNet on the TCIA-LUNG dataset and a CIRS thorax phantom dataset. STCNet performed better than conventional methods and recent deep learning baselines in image quality, artifact reduction, and structural preservation. On TCIA-LUNG, STCNet reached PSNR values of 33.311, 32.695, and 32.658 dB at phases 2, 5, and 8. The corresponding SSIM values were 0.845, 0.823, and 0.825. On CIRS, STCNet achieved PSNR values up to 36.497 dB and SSIM values up to 0.877. These results support STCNet as a promising framework for low-dose, phase-resolved 4D CBCT reconstruction in image-guided radiotherapy.

title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

title: Denoise X: Self-Supervised U-Net for Quantum Mottle Suppression in Chest Radiography
abstract: Deep learning for medical image restoration is often constrained by the need for paired training data. Acquiring perfectly registered clean-noisy radiographs in vivo is impractical due to patient motion and radiation-dose limits. To address this, we employ a self-supervised Noise2Noise paradigm that trains on independently corrupted observations without paired clean images. We propose Denoise X, a lightweight self-supervised U-Net model (7.79M parameters) for suppressing quantum mottle and electronic readout noise in low-dose chest radiographs. It is trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset (112,120 images) using a stochastic Poisson-Gaussian noise simulator. Zero-shot evaluation on the unseen Montgomery County dataset achieved a PSNR of 36.09 dB and SSIM of 0.8806, outperforming the Bilateral filter while preserving high-frequency anatomical details. Using patch-wise inference, Denoise X processes native-resolution chest radiographs in ~2.2 s per image on a Tesla P100 GPU. Cross-domain evaluation on the Shenzhen dataset achieved 36.44 dB PSNR and 0.9099 SSIM, showing strong generalization. For resource-constrained deployment, the model was converted into a 31.16 MB ONNX model for efficient CPU inference on non-DICOM images.

title: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation With Stage-Wise Shared Adapters
abstract: Different MRI modalities reveal different parts of a brain tumor. Segmentation models combine information from these modalities to outline tumor regions. Many models use a separate encoder for each modality. However, exchanging features among these encoders at several stages can increase model complexity. We introduce the Block-Wise Shared Adapter (BWSA), which combines compressed features from the modality encoders in a shared path and returns adapted features to each stream. In its fixed-blending form, BWSA adds the adapted features to the original features. Its trainable-gated variant (TG-BWSA) instead learns separate weights for the original and adapted features at each modality and encoder stage. We evaluate both variants on BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2023 with four segmentation backbones. On the official BraTS 2023 online validation set, BWSA increases average region-wise Dice by 1.3--7.6 percentage points relative to the corresponding unmodified backbones. TG-BWSA increases it by 2.8--7.7 points. Both variants add approximately 0.85--3.73% parameters and reduce average HD95 relative to the unmodified backbones.

title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning in Oncology
abstract: Deep learning has enabled substantial advances in oncology, including cancer detection and diagnosis, medical image analysis, tumor characterization, treatment planning, response assessment, and outcome prediction. However, conventional data-driven models often require large annotated datasets, exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings, and lack explicit mechanisms for incorporating the physical, physiological, and biological principles underlying cancer development and treatment. Physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) integrates governing physical laws, mechanistic models, physiological constraints, and domain knowledge into deep learning frameworks, providing a principled approach for learning from sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous oncological data. This review presents a task-oriented synthesis of PIDL methods across oncology, encompassing neural networks, Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, convolutional and vision architectures, neural operators, generative models, and hybrid physics-data-driven frameworks. Their applications are examined across cancer detection and diagnosis, image reconstruction and analysis, tumor characterization, quantitative imaging, tumor progression, treatment response, radiation therapy, treatment planning, and multimodal clinical modeling. Based on the synthesized methodological and application-level evidence, we develop task-optimized PIDL workflows that align the clinical task with appropriate data representations, physical constraints, model architectures, and validation strategies. We further analyze key challenges, including physical-model fidelity, computational scalability, uncertainty quantification, domain generalization, standardized benchmarking, and clinical validation.

title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge
abstract: International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.

title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. We use our 3D foundation model, anatomix, to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes and further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific, component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system placed first on the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at https://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

title: Personalising Deformable Image Registration with Clinical Context and Deformation History for Adaptive Radiotherapy
abstract: Adaptive radiotherapy must account for anatomical changes during treatment, but doing so depends on reliably mapping targets, organs at risk and dose across serial images. Existing registration methods treat each image pair independently, without using radiotherapy-specific context or the patient's preceding anatomical trajectory. We developed Clinical-context-Aware and Patient-adaptive Deformable Image Registration (CAP-DIR), integrating source contours, dose, clinical text and prior-registration features. We evaluated 16,361 CT examinations from 3,473 patients across four institutional cohorts and five public benchmarks. CAP-DIR increased internal-test organ-at-risk-region normalized cross-correlation from 84.76% to 96.92% relative to the strongest learning-based comparator, with low deformation folding, and remained superior across seven external cohorts. In a blinded review of 20 longitudinal cases, clinically acceptable contours increased from 45.0% to 82.5% for clinical target volumes and from 22.5% to 62.5% for organs at risk, while estimated editing time decreased. In a controlled benchmark, CAP-DIR reduced global dose-mapping error by 34.5% relative to the strongest comparator. These findings show that clinically informed, longitudinal registration can improve contour usability and dose mapping for adaptive radiotherapy.

title: DoReMe: Dual optimization of Reconstruction and Motion estimation for self-navigated free-breathing abdominal MRI using Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Purpose: Free-breathing abdominal MRI is limited by respiratory motion, which introduces image artifacts and k-space inconsistencies. Existing reconstruction approaches often depend on pre-estimated motion fields or external respiratory surrogate signals. We propose a coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm for self-navigated free-breathing acquisition, in which motion is represented by compact Gaussian primitives and jointly refined with the image estimates during iterative reconstruction. Methods: An iterative reconstruction that alternates between data consistency updates and motion modelling was proposed. Respiratory motion was represented using Gaussian primitives. A Gaussian splatting was integrated into the reconstruction algorithm. The method was evaluated on self-navigated free-breathing Cartesian gradient-echo (GRE) acquisition in four healthy volunteers, including retrospective scan shortening experiments, and was compared with regularized compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction. Results: Respiratory motion states were reconstructed in approximately 1.5 min. Compared with CS, the proposed method improved visual image quality, particularly in coronal liver views, and better preserved anatomical structures in retrospectively shortened acquisitions. These findings provide proof of concept for the proposed method. Conclusion: The proposed coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm improved visual image quality compared with CS alone. Gaussian primitives provided a compact and sufficiently flexible representation of nonrigid respiratory motion with practical runtime, supporting further scanner integration and validation in larger cohorts.

title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.

title: High-resolution retinal matrix imaging via computational motion and aberration correction
abstract: High-resolution optical imaging of the human retina is essential for diagnosing ophthalmic and neurodegenerative diseases. While adaptive optics combined with coherence gating can resolve retinal structures at the cellular scale, it requires complex, costly, and cumbersome hardware to physically correct for ocular aberrations and motion. Matrix imaging offers a powerful digital alternative by leveraging wave linearity to undo aberrations and multiple scattering; however, its in vivo deployment has been hindered by continuous, involuntary eye movements that destroy phase coherence during acquisition. Here, we overcome this fundamental barrier and demonstrate the first in vivo reflection matrix imaging of the human retina using an ultra-simplified optical setup without physical correctors. We introduce a fully computational framework that tracks and compensates for multi-axial ocular motion directly from raw interferometric data, thereby restoring the phase coherence of a multi-spectral distortion matrix. This enables local, high-order aberration correction to achieve diffraction-limited, volumetric imaging of retinal tissues. By shifting the hardware burden to physics-guided numerical computation, this paradigm opens the way for accessible, non-invasive, and high-resolution digital ophthalmology.

title: The Added Value of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in Children With Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Presenting as a Clinically Isolated Lesion.
abstract: Background The clinical utility of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in children diagnosed with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) who present with a clinically isolated lesion remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the added value of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in identifying occult lesions and assessing its impact on disease classification and clinical outcomes in this patient population. Methods This retrospective study included children who underwent surgical resection of a clinically isolated lesion, were confirmed to have LCH by histopathology, and received 18 F-FDG PET/CT prior to initiation of systemic therapy. Outcomes including detection of additional lesions, disease reclassification, and progression-free survival were analyzed. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank test was used to compare progression-free survival between groups. Results A total of 44 children were included (median age 4.29 years; 70.5% male). 18 F-FDG PET/CT identified additional lesions in 24 patients (54.5%), leading to reclassification as single-system multifocal disease in 10 (22.7%) and multisystem disease in 14 (31.8%). Four patients (9.1%) had risk organ involvement. 18 F-FDG PET/CT findings altered the treatment strategy in 54.5% of patients. All 5 relapsed patients belonged to the group with additional lesions (p = 0.044). Conclusion 18 F-FDG PET/CT detected additional lesions in over half of the children diagnosed with LCH presenting as a clinically isolated lesion, resulting in disease reclassification and improved risk stratification. 18 F-FDG PET/CT should be routinely performed in this clinical scenario to ensure accurate staging and appropriate treatment.

title: Stage-Specific Patterns of Imaging and Non-Motor Biomarkers in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3.
abstract: Objective Advancements in disease-modifying therapies for spinocerebellar ataxia Type 3 (SCA3) underscore the need for robust biomarkers to monitor disease progression and evaluate treatment efficacy. Although motor phenotypes have been well characterized, less is known about non-motor and imaging-based features across different disease stages. This study aimed to characterize stage-specific patterns of non-motor and imaging biomarkers in SCA3. Methods This cross-observational study included 229 patients with SCA3 and 104 age- and sex-matched healthy controls from the Organization for Southeast China for cerebellar ataxia research. Non-motor symptoms were assessed using a battery of neuropsychological tests. Brain volume loss was assessed by 3.0-Tesla MRI with regions-of-interest (ROI)-based volumetric analysis. Neuroinflammation was quantified in vivo using translocator protein positron emission tomography (TSPO-PET) with the 18 F-DPA-714 radioligand. Additive regression models were fitted to evaluate the cross-sectional associations between biomarkers and disease stages. Receiver operating curve (ROC) analyses were applied to estimate the discriminative ability of the candidate biomarkers. Results Non-motor symptoms, including cognitive functions, anxiety, fatigue, depression, and sleep quality, declined after ataxia onset in SCA3. Volume loss in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon diverged from normal controls at 0.7 and 0.2 years before ataxia onset, respectively. Correspondingly, the TSPO signal in the brainstem and ventral diencephalon increased and deviated from normal throughout the disease course. Interpretation Our findings propose a staging model of SCA3 that includes a biomarker stage characterized by multidimensional objective indicators of neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation from pre-ataxia to ataxia onset. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04010214.

title: The Independent and Combined Effects of Mindfulness Meditation and Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation on Central Pain Processing in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis.
abstract: Objective The Pain Relief for OsteoArthritis through Combined Treatment (PROACT) was a proof-of-principle mechanistic randomized controlled trial to examine the effects of Breathing and Attention Training (BAT), and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on pain modulatory balance, pain-related brain function, and clinical pain in middle-aged to older adults with knee osteoarthritis (OA). Methods Participants completed baseline health screening, clinical knee pain assessment, quantitative sensory testing (QST), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in response to mechanical pain evocation of the index knee. They were randomized to receive concurrent sham BAT/sham tDCS, active BAT/sham tDCS, sham BAT/active tDCS or active BAT/active tDCS. Participants completed 20-minute interventions for five consecutive days. After, participants repeated the clinical knee pain assessment, QST, and fMRI. Results Adjusted analyses of 226 completers revealed no significant main effects of treatment on clinical pain or pain modulatory balance. However, average pain-evoked cerebral blood flow across pain-related regions of interest was significantly lower for active tDCS (-3.14 [CI:-4.83- -1.45]) vs. sham tDCS (-0.51 [CI:-2.19-1.17]), though this finding did not survive multiple correction. Pre-planned follow-up comparisons revealed that the active BAT/active tDCS group showed lower post-intervention pain-evoked cerebral blood flow than the sham BAT/sham tDCS group. Conclusions The PROACT study found that mindfulness meditation in combination with tDCS may reduce pain-evoked cerebral blood flow in adults with knee OA. Future research is needed to determine if a longer duration of exposure to the combined active BAT/active tDCS treatment beneficially influences pain modulatory balance and clinical knee pain in this population.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Color Doppler Ultrasound for Detecting Nuchal Cord and Associated Immediate Neonatal Outcomes at Term in Uganda: A Prospective Diagnostic-Accuracy Cohort Study.
abstract: Background and aims Evidence on the diagnostic performance of color Doppler ultrasound for detecting nuchal cord and its association with immediate neonatal outcomes remains limited in sub-Saharan Africa. We evaluated ultrasound detection of nuchal cord and compared immediate neonatal outcomes according to nuchal-cord status. Methods This prospective study included 246 women with singleton pregnancies at ≥ 37 weeks who were enrolled in early labor at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital, Uganda, from February to July 2021. Two-dimensional and color Doppler ultrasound was performed at enrollment, and direct examination of the umbilical cord at delivery was the reference standard. Diagnostic-performance measures and unadjusted risk ratios (RRs) were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Nuchal cord was confirmed at delivery in 88/246 participants in the sampled cohort. Ultrasound identified 76/88 participants with and 152/158 without a nuchal cord. Sensitivity was 86.4% (95% CI: 77.4-92.8), specificity 96.2% (95% CI: 91.9-98.6), positive predictive value 92.7% (95% CI: 84.8-97.3) and negative predictive value 92.7% (95% CI: 87.6-96.2). Overall accuracy was 92.7% (228/246), and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.913. The composite immediate adverse neonatal outcome occurred in 18/88 neonates with a nuchal cord and 8/158 without one (20.5% vs. 5.1%; RR: 4.04, 95% CI: 1.83-8.91). Conclusion Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrated good diagnostic performance for detecting nuchal cord at term. Nuchal cord was associated with higher unadjusted risks of immediate adverse neonatal outcomes, although residual confounding cannot be excluded. Sonographic detection may inform delivery-room preparedness but should not, in isolation, determine the mode of delivery.

Nuchal cord was confirmed at delivery in 88/246 participants in the sampled cohort. Ultrasound identified 76/88 participants with and 152/158 without a nuchal cord. Sensitivity was 86.4% (95% CI: 77.4-92.8), specificity 96.2% (95% CI: 91.9-98.6), positive predictive value 92.7% (95% CI: 84.8-97.3) and negative predictive value 92.7% (95% CI: 87.6-96.2). Overall accuracy was 92.7% (228/246), and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.913. The composite immediate adverse neonatal outcome occurred in 18/88 neonates with a nuchal cord and 8/158 without one (20.5% vs. 5.1%; RR: 4.04, 95% CI: 1.83-8.91).

Conclusion

Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrated good diagnostic performance for detecting nuchal cord at term. Nuchal cord was associated with higher unadjusted risks of immediate adverse neonatal outcomes, although residual confounding cannot be excluded. Sonographic detection may inform delivery-room preparedness but should not, in isolation, determine the mode of delivery.

title: Abbreviated MRI and Ultrafast MRI of the Breast.
abstract: Detection of breast cancer in MRI requires fast, dynamic contrast enhanced (DCE) imaging covering the immediate post-contrast phase, that is, the first 60 s after contrast injection. This ensures selective depiction of invasive cancer as well as DCIS against an otherwise dark background, that is, before background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) can set in. Thus, breast MRI requires not only high spatial, but also high temporal resolution. Both, abbreviated breast MRI (AB-MRI) as well as ultrafast breast MRI (UF-MRI), exploit the fact that enhancement of cancers versus their non-cancerous background differs most in the immediate post-contrast phase. Beyond this, however, AB-MRI and UF-MRI are unrelated: AB-MRI is a novel MRI paradigm; UF-MRI is a novel MRI pulse sequence that allows time-resolved imaging of the immediate post-contrast phase. AB-MRI is an umbrella term for lean, streamlined MRI protocols designed to answer specific clinical questions. Compared with "all-purpose" full-protocol MRI, AB-MRI allows a substantial reduction of acquisition time. The first proposed use case of AB-MRI was for breast cancer screening, to reduce cost, and thus improve access and tolerability. It had been termed "FAST," short for "first post-contrast subtracted imaging," because it truncated the breast MRI acquisition protocol after one post-contrast scan covering the immediate post-contrast phase. Around the same time, UF-MRI was inaugurated. This may have caused the misunderstanding that both would represent different positions on the same line of development, with "ultrafast" being even faster than "FAST." AB-MRI protocols can be categorized into short and abridged protocols. Short protocols concentrate on the pre- and immediate post-contrast phase, either by regular DCE-MRI, or by UF-MRI. Abridged protocols add carefully selected scans, for example, T2-weighted and/or post-contrast scans. This review aims at clarifying the definitions and respective concepts of AB-MRI and UF-MRI, and to summarize the current evidence regarding the respective utility for breast cancer diagnosis.

title: MRI-Based 2.5D Multi-Instance Deep Learning for Differentiating Pathological Subtypes of Brain Metastases From Lung Cancer.
abstract: Background Distinct treatment strategies for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) brain metastases require accurate noninvasive subtyping. Purpose To develop and externally validate a biparametric MRI-based 2.5D multi-instance learning (MIL) deep learning (DL) model for discriminating SCLC from NSCLC brain metastases, with performance compared against clinical, radiomics, and 3D-DL models. Study type Retrospective. Population This study included 366 patients from four institutions. Center 1 provided the training set (n = 199; mean age, 63.88 ± 10.79 years; 72.36% male) and an internal tuning set (n = 85; mean age, 64.73 ± 9.53 years; 67.06% male). Centers 2-4 were pooled into a single external test set (n = 82; mean age, 62.26 ± 10.60 years; 63.41% male). Field strength/sequence 1.5 T and 3.0 T; contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging and fluid-attenuated inversion-recovery imaging. Assessment The 2.5D-MIL model was benchmarked against clinical, radiomics, and 3D-DL models and evaluated on internal tuning and pooled external test sets. Statistical tests Shapiro-Wilk, Student's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, chi-square, univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and DeLong tests were used. Performance measures included the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) with 95% confidence intervals and classification and calibration metrics. Statistical significance was defined as two-sided p < 0.05. Results In the internal tuning set, AUCs were 0.842 (2.5D-MIL), 0.740 (clinical), 0.710 (radiomics), and 0.747 (3D-DL). In the external test set, AUCs were 0.826 (2.5D-MIL), 0.826 (clinical), 0.696 (radiomics), and 0.664 (3D-DL). Differences between 2.5D-MIL and the clinical (p = 1.000), radiomics (p = 0.139), and 3D-DL (p = 0.119) models were not significant. Data conclusion The MRI-based 2.5D-MIL model showed potential for noninvasive differentiation of SCLC from NSCLC brain metastases. Larger prospective studies are needed before clinical use. Evidence level 3. Technical efficacy Stage 2.

title: ACR TI-RADS Modified by CEUS Features and Nodule Location for Diagnosis and Biopsy Decision in Thyroid Nodules of TR4 or Higher.
abstract: Objectives To develop a modified American College of Radiology (ACR) thyroid imaging, reporting and data system (TI-RADS) incorporating contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) features and nodule location to improve diagnostic performance and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) recommendations for ACR TR4 or higher thyroid nodules. Methods This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent ultrasound and CEUS at 3 hospitals between June 2024 and January 2026. CEUS and location features were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression to construct the modified system. Diagnostic performance and biopsy recommendation efficiency were compared with ACR TI-RADS. Results Four hundred and eight patients with 442 nodules were included. Independent predictors included enhancement intensity, enhancement direction, ring enhancement, enhancement area and nodule location. In the training set (n = 334), the modified system achieved higher AUC and sensitivity than ACR TI-RADS (AUC: 0.90 [95% CI: 0.86-0.93] versus 0.75 [95% CI: 0.71-0.79]; sensitivity: 88.5% versus 60.3%; p < .01), higher accuracy of malignant nodule biopsies (AMB: 67.1% versus 49.4%), lower unnecessary biopsy rate (UBR: 32.9% versus 50.6%), and lower biopsy rate of benign nodules (BRB: 20.8% versus 31.2%), with no unsafe downgrading. Similar results were observed in the temporal validation set (n = 108): AUC 0.95 (95% CI: 0.90-0.99) versus 0.73 (95% CI: 0.66-0.79); sensitivity 87.0% versus 49.3%; AMB 83.3% versus 53.3%; UBR 16.7% versus 46.7%, and BRB 5.1% versus 17.9%. Conclusions A modified ACR TI-RADS integrating CEUS features and nodule location improved diagnostic performance and FNA recommendations for ACR TR4 or higher nodules. Pending external validation, this system may provide a practical approach for refining risk stratification and reducing unnecessary biopsies.

title: Greater three-dimensional cam burden and superolateral location are associated with end-stage hip osteoarthritis: A retrospective comparative study.
abstract: Purpose Cam-type femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a recognised structural contributor to primary hip osteoarthritis (OA), yet many cam-positive hips do not progress to radiographic joint failure. This study aimed to compare three-dimensional cam morphology and lesion location between cam-positive hips with end-stage primary osteoarthritis and cam-positive, non-arthritic hips in an elderly fracture cohort. Methods Hospital records and imaging archives from January 2020 to January 2026 were retrospectively reviewed at a single centre. The OA group comprised patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty for primary OA, and the fracture group comprised patients aged ≥ 65 years treated for intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric femoral fractures without radiographic OA. Cam morphology was characterised using radial CT-based alpha angle, three-dimensional cam volume, cam/head volume ratio, and clock-face-based lesion location. Group comparisons, receiver operating characteristic analyses, correlation testing, and multivariable logistic regression were performed. Results A total of 438 cam-positive hips were included (126 OA and 312 fracture). OA hips demonstrated higher alpha angles (72.44° ± 5.94° vs. 62.45° ± 5.07°), larger cam volumes (5274.77 ± 1353.26 mm 3 vs. 3215.20 ± 1524.84 mm 3 ), higher cam/head ratios (8.61% ± 2.02% vs. 6.35% ± 1.97%), and more superolateral lesions (52.4% vs. 36.2% anterior in the fracture group) (all p < 0.001). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses identified cohort-specific discriminatory values of 66° for alpha angle (AUC, 0.884), 4421 mm 3 for cam volume (AUC, 0.839), and 6.4% for the cam-to-head volume ratio (AUC, 0.791). In multivariable analyses using continuous morphology measures, higher alpha angle, greater cam volume, higher cam-to-head volume ratio, and superolateral lesion location were associated with end-stage OA-group membership. Conclusions Compared with non-arthritic cam-positive hips in an elderly fracture cohort, end-stage primary OA hips had greater three-dimensional cam burden, with lesions more often located superolaterally. These retrospective associations do not establish longitudinal progression, causality, or individual prognosis. Study design Retrospective comparative study. Level of evidence Level III, study of a non-consecutive patients, study of diagnostic test.

title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

title: Integrated Multi-Time-Point <sup>18</sup>F-FAPI PET/CT and Immune Histopathology for Predicting Pathological Complete Response in Microsatellite-Stable Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer Treated With Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy, Chemotherapy, and Immunotherapy.
abstract: Predicting pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy and chemotherapy remains challenging in microsatellite-stable (MSS) locally advanced rectal cancer. In this prospective exploratory study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06608537), 49 patients received short-course radiotherapy followed by sintilimab plus CAPOX and subsequently underwent radical surgery. We investigated whether treatment response could be better characterized by integrating two complementary biological dimensions: baseline immune organization and treatment-related stromal remodeling captured by multi-time-point 1 8 F-FAPI PET/CT. The pCR rate was 49.0% (24/49), and serial 1 8 F-FAPI imaging revealed distinct stromal kinetic patterns between response groups. Integration of intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (iTLS) count, B-cell density, preoperative tumor-to-iliacus muscle ratio (TIMR) at 30 min, and the delayed TIMR retention index from 90 to 120 min (RI 34 ) yielded a four-variable model with a mean AUC of 0.874 in repeated nested cross-validation. Complementary preclinical experiments provided functional support for a CAF-TGFβ-B-cell/TLS axis linking stromal regulation, immune organization, and treatment resistance. These findings highlight the complementary value of spatial immune organization and dynamic FAPI-defined stromal kinetics and provide a biologically informed framework for post-neoadjuvant, preoperative response stratification, pending prospective multicenter validation.

title: The Bird's Nest Sign as an Initial Presentation of Primary Pulmonary B-Cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma With Plasmacytic Differentiation.
abstract: The bird's nest sign (BNS) has been described as a sign on chest computed tomography (CT) in various pulmonary diseases. We report a rare case of primary pulmonary B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation presenting with BNS, mimicking an invasive fungal disease at first. A 61-year-old Vietnamese man with a history of idiopathic thrombocytopenia and splenectomy 3 years prior to admission presented with prolonged dry cough, mild dyspnoea on exertion and chest discomfort for 3 weeks. His laboratory tests were unremarkable, but his chest CT showed bilateral consolidation with the BNS. After an unfavourable response to anti-fungal therapy, the second transthoracic lung biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of primary pulmonary B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation. This case highlights the importance of considering lymphoma in the differential diagnosis of BNS when infection is excluded and concurrently seeking a confirmatory diagnosis with repeated diagnostic procedures when necessary.

title: Recent Advances in Wearable Ultrasound Patches for Healthcare Applications.
abstract: Wearable ultrasound patches, as a transformative innovation redefining the boundaries of traditional ultrasound medicine, signify a shift from hospital-centered, episodic diagnosis and therapy toward portable, personalized, and continuous healthcare solutions. As an emerging and rapidly evolving research direction, fully integrated wearable ultrasound platforms-synergistically combining real-time imaging, closed-loop sensing, and on-demand therapeutic intervention within a single conformal patch and system-have been progressively utilized for chronic disease management and closed-loop neuromodulation. This review summarizes and discusses the advanced wearable ultrasound technologies to provide insight into the underlying strategies that enable the convergence of diagnosis and therapy in diverse disease scenarios. This review primarily focuses on wearable ultrasound patches and systems for cardiovascular monitoring, musculoskeletal assessment, neurological treatment, sonodynamic therapy, drug delivery, and integrated theranostics. In addition, the challenges and development prospects of wearable ultrasound patches are analyzed to promote further clinical translation, with emphasis on the synergistic optimization of imaging and therapy, long-term integration reliability, and fully integrated portable designs. It is earnestly expected that this kind of flexible-electronics-enabled wearable ultrasound technology will stimulate comprehensive investigation and promote the clinical development of next-generation multifunctional theranostic platforms.

title: A case report of pediatric Gardner syndrome and literature review.
abstract: This case report discusses the diagnosis and treatment of a 14-year-8-month-old male patient genetically diagnosed with Gardner syndrome (GS), systematically reviewing the disease's epidemiology, clinical manifestations, imaging advances, and management strategies. The patient presented with a post-influenza A chest wall mass and had prior resections of abdominal/scalp masses. Colonoscopy revealed > 20 adenomatous polyps. Imaging demonstrated multiple craniofacial osteomas and epidermoid cysts. Genetic testing identified a pathogenic APC gene mutation (NM_000038.6:c.4669_4670del (p.Ile1557*) heterozygous variant). GS, a familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) subtype, has an estimated pediatric incidence of 1/8000-1/14,000. Its classic triad comprises colorectal polyps, osteomas, and soft tissue tumors. Recent studies indicate earlier malignant transformation of duodenal polyps in children versus adults, with desmoid tumor incidence reaching 10-20%. In imaging, low-dose CT, panoramic radiography, and contrast-enhanced MRI can improve early detection of bone lesions and soft tissue tumors. Genetic testing (APC/MUTYH) is the pediatric screening gold standard. Optimized chemoprevention (sulindac/celecoxib) and endoscopic monitoring have significantly improved prognoses. This case highlights the urgency of multidisciplinary management and genetic counseling for pediatric GS.

title: Machine learning-assisted monitoring of radiofrequency ablation in hepatic tumors using spectral traces.
abstract: Purpose Accurate intraoperative assessment of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) margins in hepatic malignancies remains a significant clinical challenge. Methods This study investigates the efficacy of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for objective, spatially resolved discrimination of ablated tissue, viable tumor, and normal parenchyma in 10 ex vivo liver specimens. Analysis of visible-near-infrared (VNIR) reflectance revealed distinct spectral signatures, characterized by a consistent monotonic hierarchy (ablated < normal < tumor), enabling reliable tissue differentiation. Segmentation performance was systematically evaluated using four supervised classifiers: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The total delineated tissue area exhibited notable inter-method variability, ranging from 137,283 to 189,289 pixels (+ 37.9%), underscoring sensitivity to classifier architecture. Results Nevertheless, all approaches maintained biologically coherent tissue distributions, with normal parenchyma predominating (44-56%), followed by tumor (25-39%) and ablated regions (17-20%). That is consistently indicating the necessity for monitoring ablative margins. SAM, SVM, and LDA classifiers achieved class-specific detection errors around 3.5% and 18%. LDA attained the highest overall accuracy (94.5%), demonstrating the potential of HSI for reliable, intraoperative image-guided tissue characterization. Dimensionality reduction across 462 spectral bands identified an optimal discriminative window within 643-698 nm, supporting the development of streamlined multispectral systems. Conclusion Overall, HSI is neither a contact nor destructive modality for quantitative RFA assessment. Despite classifier-dependent variability necessitating standardized or ensemble strategies, these findings support its prospective integration into real-time surgical guidance, pending in vivo validation.

title: Predicting advanced-stage recurrence in resected hepatocellular carcinoma using preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI radiomics.
abstract: Objectives To develop and validate a preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI-based radiomics model for predicting the time to advanced-stage recurrence in patients undergoing resection for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included patients with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage 0/A HCC who underwent resection between 2009 and 2014. Patients were temporally divided into training (n = 272; 2009-2011) and validation (n = 210; 2012-2014) cohorts. Time to advanced-stage recurrence was defined as the interval from resection to macrovascular invasion and/or extrahepatic metastasis. Two radiologists segmented tumors on hepatobiliary phase images, followed by 3-mm peritumoral expansion and propagation to co-registered dynamic T1- and T2-weighted images. After extraction of Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative-compliant features, a radiomics model was developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox regression. Model performance and inter-reader reproducibility of binary risk stratification were evaluated using the concordance index (C-index) and Cohen's kappa, respectively. Results Five-year advanced-stage recurrence occurred in 15% of the training (42/272) and validation (32/210) cohorts. In the validation cohort, the radiomics model yielded a C-index of 0.716 (95% CI, 0.631-0.801). This outperformed the preoperative BCLC (0.597; 95% CI 0.551-0.644) and Hong Kong Liver Cancer (0.594; 95% CI 0.516-0.672) staging systems, and was equivalent to the postoperative clinicopathological model (0.716; 95% CI 0.626-0.807). Radiomic-based risk stratification showed good inter-reader reproducibility (kappa = 0.757). Conclusion The preoperative radiomics model outperformed staging systems and was comparable to the postoperative clinicopathological model in predicting advanced-stage recurrence, relying entirely on noninvasive data.

title: Limited incremental value and cross-cohort transferability of CT radiomics for survival prediction after TACE in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether pretreatment CT radiomics adds information for overall survival (OS) prediction among patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and assess frozen imaging-model performance in an independent cohort. Methods This retrospective study included 221 WAW-TACE and 98 HCC-TACE-SEG patients with pretreatment arterial and portal venous CT. Incremental value of a tumor-radiomics Random Survival Forest score (R1) beyond cohort-specific clinical Cox models (C0) was evaluated within each cohort using 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times. External validation was restricted to frozen WAW-trained R1 models (Top-K = 5, 10, 15) applied to HCC-TACE-SEG without refitting; the combined C0 + R1 model was not externally validated. Results WAW-TACE included 162 deaths and HCC-TACE-SEG 86 deaths. In WAW-TACE, C0, R1 Top-K = 15, and C0 + R1 achieved C-indices of 0.646 ± 0.043, 0.593 ± 0.049, and 0.639 ± 0.045, respectively. Corresponding HCC-TACE-SEG estimates were 0.496 ± 0.087, 0.530 ± 0.072, and 0.495 ± 0.094. Thus, R1 did not consistently improve cohort-specific clinical reference models. In frozen external application, Top-K = 5, 10, and 15 achieved C-indices of 0.463 (95% CI 0.397-0.532), 0.535 (0.468-0.608), and 0.528 (0.460-0.598), respectively. Conclusion The evaluated models showed no consistent incremental value for OS prediction within these TACE cohorts and limited frozen-model discrimination in the clinically distinct HCC-TACE-SEG cohort. These findings do not support clinical use of these models or establish a general limitation of CT radiomics.

title: Restaging the primary tumor in localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma after systemic therapy: a scoping review of the role of CT, FDG-PET, and CA19-9.
abstract: Objectives The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates. Materials and methods This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL. Results Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies. Conclusion Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue. Key points Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

title: Atypical presacral masses in Currarino syndrome: a case series.
abstract: Introduction Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. While anterior meningoceles and teratomas are the most commonly reported lesions, an expanding body of literature suggests a broader spectrum of presacral pathology. We present three cases from our institution that expand the phenotypic range of presacral masses associated with Currarino syndrome, including lesions not previously well described in this population. Case presentation Three cases are presented. Final pathologic diagnoses included myxopapillary ependymoma, mature cystic teratoma, and neuroendocrine tumor arising within a teratoma. Conclusion These cases highlight the considerable heterogeneity of presacral lesions in Currarino syndrome and identify two underrecognized or previously unreported tumor types: myxopapillary ependymoma and neuroendocrine tumor. Surgical management must be individualized and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Future studies will further clarify genotype-phenotype relationships and improve diagnostic and management strategies in this complex syndrome. Established facts Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. Presacral masses are most commonly anterior meningoceles and teratomas. A wider spectrum of lesions has been reported, underscoring the complexity of the syndrome and the importance of thorough evaluation and management of presacral pathology. Novel insights In Case 1, we report a previously undescribed association of myxopapillary ependymoma with a retrorectal teratoma in the setting of Currarino syndrome. Case 2 illustrates the potential for significant enlargement of presacral meningoceles with associated teratomas with a rare instance of prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound. Case 3 expands the spectrum of presacral pathology in Currarino syndrome by demonstrating a neuroendocrine tumor.

title: Notch-referenced mediolateral verification of tibial tunnel position in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a 3D imaging validation study.
abstract: Background Non-anatomic tibial tunnel placement remains a leading contributor to anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) failure. Mediolateral (ML) tunnel positioning is particularly difficult intraoperatively because no consistent bony landmark defines the lateral footprint border. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of a novel intraoperative Notch-Referenced Mediolateral (NRML) verification technique by comparing the ML position of the tibial tunnel center (TTC) on postoperative 3D CT with the native tibial footprint center (TFC) on preoperative 3D MRI. Methods In this retrospective cross-sectional study, 108 consecutive patients underwent primary all-inside single-bundle ACLR with intraoperative NRML verification. This arthroscopic technique uses the intercondylar notch as a visual reference to verify mediolateral tibial tunnel position before definitive drilling. TFC and TTC were independently measured on preoperative 3D MRI and postoperative 3D CT using a standardized quadrant-grid protocol by two blinded observers. The primary outcome was ML deviation (tunnel - footprint). MRI-CT agreement and measurement reliability were assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis. Results The anatomical TFC was located at 46.1 ± 2.3% of tibial plateau width in the ML direction, versus 44.8 ± 2.0% for the TTC. Mean ML deviation was -1.01 ± 1.52 mm (p < 0.001), a small but statistically significant medial bias; 91.7% (95% CI 84.9-95.6%) of tunnels fell within ±3 mm of the native footprint. MRI-CT agreement was good (ICC 0.81-0.85), and inter/intraobserver reliability was good to excellent (ICC 0.78-0.89). No significant associations were found between ML deviation and sex, injury chronicity, graft diameter, or plateau size. Conclusion In this single-arm cohort,NRML verification is a simple, equipment-free technique that placed the tibial tunnel within ~1 mm of the native ML footprint, with high measurement reliability. Prospective comparative and outcome studies are needed to confirm its clinical value. Level of evidence IV.
